Because it skipped only under high torque in the smallest rear cog, treat it as a drivetrain fault until proven otherwise. Do not reproduce the skip by riding or by applying heavy resistance on a work stand.

1. Make the bicycle safe

- Put it in a stable repair stand, or support it securely with the rear wheel off the ground.
- Do not use an e-bike motor. Remove or disable the battery if applicable.
- Keep fingers, clothing, and tools clear of the chain and sprockets.
- Rotate the cranks only by hand, slowly.

2. Check wheel seating and axle security first

- Confirm the rear wheel is fully seated in both dropouts.
- For a thru-axle, verify it is fully threaded and tightened to the bicycle’s specified torque.
- For a quick release, confirm the lever is firmly closed—not merely resting against the frame.
- Hold the rim at the 3-and-9-o’clock positions and then 6-and-12-o’clock positions. Try to move it sideways.
  - No perceptible play: good sign.
  - Any clicking, sideways movement, shifting in the dropouts, or axle that can be turned by hand: stop and have it serviced.
- Spin the wheel slowly and check that it does not visibly wobble or rub the frame.

A loose wheel can change chain alignment and must be corrected before any further diagnosis.

3. Check the cassette and freehub for movement

With the wheel installed:

- Watch the cassette while slowly rotating the cranks backward.
- The sprocket stack should run true, without obvious side-to-side wobble.
- Carefully try to move the sprocket stack sideways relative to the wheel. It should not have perceptible play.
- If the wheel stays still but the cassette moves, or you hear a click from the cassette area, suspect a loose cassette lockring, loose freehub, or freehub bearing problem.

Do not simply tighten the lockring by feel unless you have the correct cassette tool, torque wrench, and the manufacturer’s torque specification. Any cassette or freehub movement is a reason to leave the bicycle unridden for a shop.

4. Inspect the chain and sprocket teeth

Clean enough dirt from the chain and cassette to see the metal clearly. Look for:

- Cracked, bent, or damaged chain plates
- A missing or damaged roller
- A bent or poorly seated quick link
- A tooth that is broken, badly burred, or visibly shorter than its neighbors
- Hooked or “shark-fin” tooth profiles, especially on the smallest rear cog
- A small cog whose teeth look substantially more pointed or asymmetric than those on less-used cogs

Pay particular attention to the smallest cog because the problem occurred only there. A worn chain combined with a worn small cog commonly skips only when torque is high.

Do not file or reshape a damaged tooth.

5. Check chain wear

Use a chain-wear gauge at several different sections of the chain, not only at one link. Follow the gauge manufacturer’s replacement markings.

- A chain beyond its replacement limit may skip on a worn cassette.
- If the chain is worn and the cassette has substantial use, replacing only the chain may not solve the problem; the small cog or the cassette may also be worn.
- If chain age and service history are unknown, have the chain and cassette assessed together.

A ruler can provide a rough indication, but a proper gauge is preferable because replacement thresholds vary by drivetrain.

6. Look for a stiff or seized link

Slowly backpedal the crank while watching the derailleur cage and chain:

- A stiff link often makes the derailleur cage jump or pulse once per chain revolution.
- The chain may become tight and then suddenly slack as the link passes through the derailleur pulleys.
- A stiff quick link may produce the same symptom.

Stop with the suspect link between the chainrings and cassette. Flex that link gently side-to-side and compare it with neighboring links. It should articulate freely without a click or tight spot.

Do not force a visibly damaged link. A stiff link that cannot be corrected confidently is a reason not to ride until the chain is repaired or replaced.

7. Check shifting and indexing with hand rotation

Starting in a larger rear cog:

- Rotate the cranks slowly by hand.
- Shift one click at a time toward the smallest cog.
- Allow the chain to settle fully after each shift.
- In the smallest cog, inspect the chain from above. It should be centered on the cog, not trying to ride the adjacent cog or drift outward.
- Listen for persistent rattling, repeated attempts to climb to the next cog, or delayed shifts.

Interpretation:

- Chain will not fully reach the smallest cog, or sits partly between two cogs: possible excessive cable tension, incorrect limit adjustment, cable/housing friction, or derailleur-hanger alignment.
- Chain reaches the smallest cog but rattles and repeatedly moves toward the next cog: indexing or hanger alignment is suspect.
- Shifts cleanly and sits centered in every cog, but the small cog still has visibly worn teeth: cog/chain wear becomes more likely.
- Shifting looks perfect by hand but the bicycle previously skipped under hard load: that does not clear the drivetrain. A worn cog or marginal engagement can behave normally without load.

Do not use barrel-adjuster changes to mask a cassette, wheel, or chain problem. If adjustment is needed, record the original position or have a shop set it up.

8. Check derailleur alignment more critically

A derailleur or hanger can be slightly misaligned without looking obviously bent.

- From behind the bicycle, compare the jockey-wheel cage with the cassette sprockets.
- In each gear, the upper jockey wheel should sit directly below the selected cog.
- Look for a cage that is angled oddly, a derailleur that contacts the spokes, or a hanger that does not appear parallel to the cassette.

Visual inspection cannot reliably confirm hanger alignment; a shop uses an alignment gauge. A suspected hanger problem, especially after any impact or wheel-removal incident, supports leaving the bicycle unridden.

Likely findings

- Indexing/cable/hanger issue: poor or delayed shifts, chain not centered on a cog, noise or attempted movement toward an adjacent cog.
- Stiff link: derailleur cage pulses or chain tightens/slackens at one repeating point.
- Worn chain or cog: chain and small-cog teeth are worn, shifting may look normal, and skipping appears mainly under torque in one frequently used cog.
- Loose wheel: rim or wheel moves relative to the frame.
- Loose cassette/freehub: wheel is secure but the cassette stack has play or wobbles.

Leave it unridden and arrange a shop inspection if any of these apply:

- The wheel, axle, cassette, or freehub has perceptible play.
- The axle or quick release cannot be confirmed secure.
- The chain has a damaged plate, missing roller, cracked link, seized link, or suspect quick link.
- Any cassette tooth is broken or badly damaged.
- The chain is beyond its wear limit, especially with an old or visibly hooked cassette.
- The derailleur hanger may be misaligned.
- The chain skips again during even a gentle, unloaded hand-rotation check.
- The cause remains uncertain after inspection.
- The skip occurred under load and no definite correction has been made and verified.

Given the reported load-dependent skips, the safest practical outcome is to have a shop check chain wear, the smallest cog/cassette, cassette lockring and freehub play, rear-wheel security, and derailleur-hanger alignment before returning the bicycle to service.

The simultaneous wired and 5 GHz stalls, followed by a WAN renegotiation from 1 Gbps to 100 Mbps, point first to the short modem-to-router Ethernet path—not to Wi-Fi interference. The normal optical-status light is useful evidence that the modem/ONT remained online, but it does not rule out a failing Ethernet cable, connector, or port.

Least-disruptive sequence:

1. Preserve evidence before changing anything

   - Record the local time of the stall.
   - Save or photograph the router log entries showing the WAN link changing from 1 Gbps to 100 Mbps, and any subsequent link-up/down messages.
   - Note whether the modem’s online/optical indicators stayed normal.
   - Record the router’s current WAN negotiated speed, duplex, uptime, and—if available—CRC, alignment, or interface errors.
   - Do not reboot the modem or factory-reset either device yet; that would remove useful timing evidence.

2. Inspect the existing connection without interrupting service

   - Check both plugs for a broken latch, bent contacts, looseness, dust, or strain.
   - Make sure the cable is not sharply bent, pinched, pulled sideways, or resting under the modem/router.
   - Confirm it is a full eight-conductor Cat5e-or-better cable. Some old or damaged cables work at 100 Mbps but cannot reliably maintain 1 Gbps.
   - Reseat both ends once, without changing router settings. Confirm the router returns to a 1 Gbps WAN link and remains there for at least 30–60 minutes of ordinary traffic.

3. Substitute only the cable

   - Use a short, known-good Cat5e, Cat6, or better cable—not a visually similar cable of unknown quality.
   - Leave the modem, router, ports, power, and settings unchanged.
   - Replace the cable while traffic is quiet; a brief interruption is expected.
   - Confirm the negotiated speed returns to 1 Gbps.
   - Keep the old cable labeled rather than discarding it, in case the ISP or technician wants it for comparison.
   - Observe the connection through normal use. If the problem disappears for a meaningful observation period, the original cable or its connector is the leading suspect.

4. Check the router WAN port

   - Inspect the router’s WAN port for looseness or damaged contacts.
   - Ensure the new cable clicks firmly into place and is not under mechanical tension.
   - If the router supports assigning another physical port as WAN, use that only if the configuration is documented and easily reversible. Do not move the cable to an ordinary LAN port at random.
   - Compare the link speed and error counters on the original WAN port with the alternate port.
   - If the alternate WAN-capable port remains stable while the original port repeatedly falls to 100 Mbps, the router WAN port is likely at fault.

5. Check the modem/ONT Ethernet port

   - Inspect the port and plug for the same physical issues.
   - If the modem/ONT has a second documented Ethernet port, test it only if the manufacturer or ISP confirms that it is active and equivalent. Many modems expose only one usable Internet port.
   - Do not change modem Ethernet settings, force a speed, or disable autonegotiation unless instructed by the ISP. Gigabit autonegotiation should normally be left enabled at both ends.

6. Collect logs during a recurrence

   On the router, capture:

   - Exact timestamp of every WAN link-down, link-up, or speed change.
   - Negotiated speed and duplex before and after the event.
   - Interface error, CRC, or symbol-error counters, if available.
   - Whether the router itself rebooted or merely lost the WAN link.

   On the modem/ONT, capture:

   - Online/optical status and uptime.
   - Ethernet-port status, negotiated speed, and Ethernet errors, if shown.
   - Event log entries at the same timestamps.
   - Any downstream/upstream, optical-level, or signal warnings.

   The important distinction is whether the modem/ONT itself lost service or whether only its Ethernet interface changed speed. A normal optical/online state with a router-side 1 Gbps-to-100 Mbps transition strongly favors the local Ethernet segment.

7. Run a controlled stability check

   After the known-good cable is installed:

   - Keep Devika’s charting and other important work on the stable connection; do not deliberately provoke an outage during use.
   - Check the WAN speed periodically rather than rebooting repeatedly.
   - If it recurs, note whether both wired and 5 GHz devices stall again, and whether the router log records the same Ethernet renegotiation.
   - A single stable hour is encouraging but not conclusive; several hours or a normal day of use without a speed change is stronger evidence.

8. Defer a direct-modem test until necessary

   Connecting a laptop directly to the modem/ONT can help isolate the router, but it is more disruptive and may require releasing a DHCP lease, renewing an ISP-assigned address, or cloning the router’s MAC address. Do this only during a maintenance window, with the ISP’s instructions, or after the cable and router-port tests point toward the modem side. It is not the first step.

Contact the ISP when any of these occurs:

   - The WAN repeatedly renegotiates to 100 Mbps or drops entirely with a known-good cable.
   - The behavior persists across a second documented WAN-capable router port.
   - The modem/ONT Ethernet port reports errors, cannot hold 1 Gbps with a known-good endpoint, or shows repeated Ethernet link events.
   - A direct-to-modem test reproduces the issue with a known-good laptop and cable.
   - The modem/ONT’s online or optical status changes, or its event log shows service loss at the same timestamps.
   - The issue recurs often enough to affect work, especially if you have timestamps showing simultaneous client stalls and corresponding modem/router events.

Give the ISP a concise evidence packet:

   - Service address/account and modem/ONT model and serial number.
   - Exact dates and local timestamps.
   - Router log showing 1 Gbps → 100 Mbps renegotiation.
   - Modem/ONT status and event-log captures from the same period.
   - Cable type and the result with the known-good replacement.
   - Which router WAN port was used and whether another documented port was tested.
   - Whether the modem/ONT remained online and whether a direct test reproduced the problem.
   - The prior successful baseline: the wired test reached about 932 Mbps down and 38 Mbps up after installation.

Ask the ISP specifically to check the modem/ONT Ethernet interface, provisioning/firmware, Ethernet error counters, and line or optical history—and to replace or test the modem/ONT if the fault follows the modem-side port. Avoid accepting a generic “signal looks normal” conclusion: that addresses the provider line, but not necessarily an Ethernet-interface failure.

Because the clasp failed to close automatically, do not use that leash with Kibo. A clasp used for restraint must close completely and reliably without hand assistance every time; retire the leash from animal use and use the intact backup.

Safe cleaning and unloaded test:

1. Keep the leash disconnected from Kibo and set it aside.
2. Rinse the clasp with clean, lukewarm fresh water to remove slush, salt, and grit. Work the spring gate open and closed under the rinse.
3. Use a soft toothbrush or cloth around the hinge and gate. Do not use a metal pick, abrasive cleaner, bleach, or solvent.
4. Shake out the water and let the clasp dry completely at room temperature. Do not heat it or apply WD-40, grease, or oil unless the manufacturer specifically directs it.
5. Inspect the gate, hinge, spring, nose, and attachment hardware for grit, rust, looseness, distortion, or cracking. Do not disassemble it.
6. With the leash unloaded and held away from Kibo, open the gate fully and release it repeatedly—at least 10–20 times—in several orientations. Each time it should snap fully shut, sit flush against the nose, and remain closed during gentle hand movement.
7. If it sticks, closes only partway, needs a push, leaves a visible gap, or behaves inconsistently even once, discard or replace the clasp/leash. Do not “test” it by attaching it to Kibo or applying pulling force.

Cleaning may remove debris, but it does not make a previously unreliable restraint safe to trust.

Preservation-first sequence:

1. Freeze the current state

   - Do not delete anything from iCloud.
   - Do not reduce the iCloud Backup scope, turn off Messages in iCloud, sign out, erase the phone, or install a major iOS update yet.
   - Leave the phone connected to power and avoid changing or deleting messages, settings, or app data while the backup runs.
   - Keep the phone’s passcode available; you may need it to approve the computer.

2. Prepare the computer and backup password

   - Confirm the computer has substantially more free space than the phone is using.
   - Use a direct, reliable USB or USB-C cable, preferably connected directly to the computer.
   - Create a strong encryption password specifically for this backup. Save it in your password manager and in a second secure offline location. Apple cannot recover an encrypted local-backup password.
   - If the computer already contains an older local backup, preserve it first: in Finder or Apple Devices, open Manage Backups, right-click the old backup, and choose Archive rather than deleting or overwriting it.

3. Connect and establish trust

   - Connect the iPhone to the computer.
   - On a Mac running macOS Catalina or later, open Finder and select the iPhone in the sidebar.
   - On Windows, open the Apple Devices app; use iTunes on older Windows installations or macOS Mojave and earlier.
   - If prompted, choose Allow or Trust on the computer and Trust on the iPhone, then enter the iPhone passcode.

4. Configure encryption before starting

   - In Finder or Apple Devices, open the General tab. In iTunes, open Summary.
   - Select “Back up all of the data on your iPhone to this Mac/Computer.”
   - Select “Encrypt local backup.”
   - Set and confirm the backup password.
   - Do not start an unencrypted backup first. Encryption is needed for items such as saved passwords, Wi-Fi settings, Health and Activity data, call history, and other sensitive settings.

5. Create the backup

   - Click Back Up Now.
   - Keep the phone connected, unlocked if requested, and powered during the entire process.
   - Do not use the computer to move or copy the backup directory while the backup is running.
   - Wait until the application reports completion and shows a new “Latest Backup” date and time. If it reports an error, do not free cloud storage; resolve the error and retry.

6. Verify the backup in the backup manager

   - Reopen Manage Backups.
   - Confirm that:
     - The device identifier/name is the intended iPhone.
     - The timestamp is from immediately after this backup run.
     - A lock icon appears beside the backup, indicating encryption.
     - The backup is present after closing and reopening Finder, Apple Devices, or iTunes.
   - If available, choose Show in Finder or Show in Explorer and confirm that the backup folder exists and has a substantial, plausible size. Do not edit its contents.

7. Preserve a second copy

   - After the backup has completed, close the backup application and copy the complete backup folder to a separate encrypted external drive or other separately protected storage.
   - Keep the original computer copy intact.
   - Label both copies with the device, date, and “encrypted local backup.”
   - Store the encryption password separately from both backup copies.
   - If you archive the backup in Finder, do so after completion so routine future backups cannot overwrite it.

8. Perform the strongest practical verification

   - The lock icon and successful completion verify that an encrypted backup was created, but they do not prove every item can be restored.
   - If you have a spare iPhone or an erased test device, restore the backup to that device and verify representative items: messages, device settings, contacts, photos that are supposed to be local, Health data, and app data. Do not erase the current phone merely to test restoration unless you have already made and preserved the backup copies.
   - If no test device is available, retain the original and second copy, verify the lock/timestamp in the backup manager, and record the password and backup location. Treat that as operational verification rather than a complete restore test.

9. Only after verification, address the cloud quota

   - First confirm that the local backup is encrypted, current, visible after reopening the backup application, and preserved in a second location.
   - Then decide whether to delete older cloud backups, free other cloud storage, or change the cloud-backup scope.
   - Do not assume that a local backup replaces cloud-synced data: items already synchronized to iCloud may not be duplicated in the computer backup. In this case, leave the current cloud backup untouched until you have specifically confirmed that the messages and settings you need are represented in the preserved local backup or otherwise retained.

Important limitation: an encrypted local backup does not include Face ID/Touch ID data, Apple Pay information, or the device passcode itself. Apps and some content already synchronized through iCloud or synced from a computer may also not be contained in the local backup.

A lone $1 pending authorization can be a harmless verification hold, but it is also a common card-testing pattern. Because you did not authorize it, use containment without assuming the account is fully compromised.

Immediate containment

1. Lock/freeze the card in the card app now.
   - Locking is proportionate here because the transaction is unrecognized and the physical card is still with you.
   - A lock may not cancel an authorization already submitted, so it may remain pending or later fall off.
   - It also may not stop every recurring, digital-wallet, or previously authorized transaction, depending on the issuer.

2. Do not attempt the transaction, contact the merchant, or use any phone number or link associated with the authorization.

3. Check briefly for:
   - Additional pending or posted charges
   - Digital-wallet cards or recently added devices
   - Authorized users
   - Recent subscriptions, trials, or card-on-file purchases that could plausibly explain a $1 hold

4. Keep the card locked while you verify it with the issuer. If another attempt appears, or the $1 charge posts, leave it locked and request replacement.

Independent issuer-contact and verification

5. Contact the issuer using only:
   - The phone number printed on the physical card
   - The issuer’s official app or website opened independently
   - A verified statement or account page—not a text, email, search-ad phone number, or merchant-provided contact

6. Tell the issuer plainly:
   - “I have an unrecognized pending $1 authorization from NORTHSTAR DIGITAL at 8:41 PM on January 17.”
   - You made no purchase at that time.
   - The physical card is in your possession.
   - You see no other unfamiliar activity.
   - Ask whether they can identify the underlying merchant, payment channel, wallet token, merchant category, or card-not-present indicator.

7. Ask what they recommend specifically for a pending authorization:
   - Whether it can be blocked or canceled
   - Whether it will automatically expire
   - When it becomes eligible for a fraud dispute if it posts
   - Whether the card number should be closed and replaced now
   - Whether any digital-wallet tokens or card-on-file tokens need to be revoked

8. Verify independently that the issuer has your correct phone number, email, mailing address, and MFA methods. If anything is wrong, report possible account takeover. Since your login and MFA still work, avoid making unrelated changes unless the issuer identifies a broader compromise; changing the app password and signing out other sessions is reasonable if you see any suspicious login or profile activity.

Evidence to preserve

This sounds consistent with mild salt-related contact irritation, given the limited pinkness and absence of a cut, swelling, heat, pain, or limp. Home care is reasonable for now, with close observation.

Paw-cleaning plan

1. Rinse the affected paw—and preferably all four paws—with lukewarm water. Let water run gently between the toes and pads for a few minutes to dissolve salt; do not scrub.
2. If salt is still visible, use a small amount of mild, fragrance-free dog shampoo, then rinse it completely. Plain water is sufficient if the paw is only mildly pink.
3. Check between the pads and around the nails for trapped granules, but do not dig at anything embedded.
4. Pat dry carefully, especially between the toes. Avoid hot air, vigorous rubbing, alcohol, hydrogen peroxide, essential oils, or human creams.
5. Prevent prolonged licking while the paw dries—supervise him, offer a quiet chew or toy, and use a cone only if necessary. Licking can keep the skin irritated and can lead to salt ingestion.

Protection for the next several days

- Keep walks short and use the least-salted route or a cleared, salt-free area until the pinkness has resolved.
- Before a walk, apply a thin layer of a dog-specific paw balm or wax to the pads and between the toes. Avoid products with fragrances, essential oils, or medication unless your veterinarian recommends them. Wipe off residue after the walk so he cannot consume much of it.
- Consider properly fitted dog booties for salted routes. Introduce them indoors gradually, and remove them immediately after the walk to check for rubbing, moisture, or trapped salt.
- After every outdoor trip, wipe or rinse his paws and dry them. Prevent him from eating salt, treated snow, or meltwater.
- Take a photo tonight so you can compare the color and appearance tomorrow.

Veterinary timing

Contact his regular veterinarian if:

- The pinkness is spreading or not clearly improving within 24–48 hours.
- Licking continues despite cleaning and route changes, or the irritation persists beyond about 48–72 hours.
- A crack, blister, raw area, discharge, odor, bleeding, swelling, warmth, or increasing tenderness develops.
- He begins limping, holding the paw up, refusing walks, or resists gentle handling.

Seek same-day or emergency advice for severe pain, rapidly increasing swelling, inability to bear weight, a deep/open wound, or marked tissue discoloration.

Because he licked a paw that had contacted fresh salt, also call a veterinarian or animal poison service promptly if he may have swallowed more than a small residue or licked treated slush/product directly. Watch for drooling, repeated vomiting or diarrhea, unusual thirst, weakness, wobbliness, tremors, seizures, or collapse. Do not induce vomiting unless a veterinarian specifically directs you.

Sources: ASPCA ice-melt guidance; VCA winter paw-protection guidance.

The increase most likely means the second progression exceeded your current flexor-pronator load tolerance. The important signal is not just the 3/10 during the final set, but that symptoms were still present the next morning; that means the dose was not yet fully tolerated. Load-monitoring guidance generally recommends modifying the load when next-day symptoms are worse, rather than progressing further.[1][2] This does not, by itself, suggest a tear—your preserved motion, ordinary grip, and absence of swelling, bruising, weakness, or sensory symptoms are reassuring—but it cannot rule out every problem remotely.

Recommendation:

1. Do not repeat or advance the second progression.
2. Let the 1/10 residual discomfort return to your usual baseline—ideally with painless ordinary use—before loading again. A short pause of a day or two is reasonable if needed.
3. Then return to the prior tolerated load, not complete rest. Keep loaded underclings and hard gripping excluded.
4. Use the next 2–3 sessions as a reassessment period. Keep symptoms at the previously prescribed low level and require no increase later that day or the next morning. If the prior load also produces a next-morning flare, stop that exercise and contact the prescribing clinician or therapist before continuing.

I would not wait until February 20 to contact the clinician if the next-morning discomfort is not clearly settling within 24–48 hours, recurs at the prior tolerated dose, or prevents you from following the plan. It would also be reasonable—but not urgent—to send the clinician a brief update now: “Second progression caused 3/10 during the last set and 1/10 the next morning; no loss of motion, grip, swelling, bruising, numbness, or tingling. I have stepped back and am excluding underclings/hard gripping. Should I resume progression one only after symptoms return to baseline?”

Seek prompt in-person assessment for new weakness, loss of grip or motion, increasing swelling/bruising, severe or worsening pain, a pop or snap, deformity/color change, or numbness/tingling.[3]

Sources:
[1] https://www.ohsu.edu/sites/default/files/2019-04/01-Walsh_0.pdf — Tendon pain - an update on mechanisms and rehabilitation
[2] https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/17307888 — Pain-monitoring model study; evidence is from Achilles tendinopathy, so applying its 24-hour principle to your wrist is an extrapolation
[3] https://www.nhs.uk/symptoms/hand-pain/wrist-pain — NHS: Wrist pain

Anya, use this bounded sequence and keep the migration script disabled until it completes:

1. Freeze the state

   - Do not modify the canonical package, generated iOS file, or committed outputs.
   - Record the current package commit and content digest, the iOS file hash, and the two timestamps that prompted the proposal.
   - Keep publication and any automatic rewrite behavior blocked.

2. Verify the generator actually used

   Capture from the lockfile, build manifest, and executable—not just configuration:

   - Exact generator version
   - Immutable generator digest or commit
   - Runtime version
   - Dependency lockfile
   - Generator configuration and target
   - Any cache or incremental-build setting

   Confirm that the generation log reports the same tuple. If the declared version and logged version differ, stop and classify this as toolchain/workflow drift.

3. Verify the canonical package commit

   - Confirm the repository commit and that the working tree was clean.
   - Hash the canonical machine-readable package at that commit.
   - Read the affected values directly from the canonical package, including alias resolution and any relevant metadata.
   - Confirm that the generation job claims that same commit/digest as its input.

   Do not infer source chronology from filesystem timestamps.

4. Inspect the generation logs

   Look for:

   - Canonical input commit/digest
   - Generator and runtime versions
   - Configuration and target
   - Cache hit, cache invalidation, or incremental-generation messages
   - Warnings about skipped or partial output
   - Complete expected output set
   - Exit status and drift-check result

   If the logs do not establish those facts, regenerate from the recorded canonical commit into a brand-new disposable directory with caches bypassed or cleared only in that disposable environment.

5. Perform a clean comparison

   Generate all three platform outputs from the unchanged canonical package using the verified generator tuple. Compare the fresh iOS output—not the existing checkout copy—against:

   - The committed iOS representation
   - The previously observed iOS file
   - The value directly read from the canonical package

   Also record exact file hashes and, where appropriate, semantic token values. Do not “fix” a difference by copying one representation over another.

6. Run the drift check

   Run the normal drift check over all generated outputs. Interpret the result as follows:

   - Fresh output matches the canonical package and the drift check passes: the existing iOS file was stale or produced through a different path; replace it only through the normal regeneration/promotion workflow.
   - Fresh output differs because the current generator/configuration differs: investigate generator or dependency drift.
   - Fresh output consistently differs while the canonical package contains the expected value: investigate the iOS generator, target mapping, or cache behavior.
   - The canonical package itself contains the unexpected value: that is the only branch that supports a source-level package investigation. It still requires an approved canonical-package change followed by regeneration of every output.

Why not write generated iOS values back into the canonical package:

- A generated file is a downstream representation, not an independent authority.
- “Newer” timestamps usually describe a write, copy, cache, checkout, or packaging event; they do not prove newer semantic data or authorship.
- Reverse-writing can overwrite correct canonical data with a platform-specific rendering and may lose aliases, metadata, types, naming semantics, or information not represented in iOS.
- It creates a circular pipeline in which an output can silently become the next source, hiding generator, cache, or configuration defects.
- It can make the three teams consume inconsistent values and undermine reproducibility, auditability, and the drift check.

The decision boundary is therefore: update the canonical package only when there is source-level evidence that its semantic value is wrong and an approved source change exists. Otherwise, preserve the canonical package, diagnose the generator/input path, and regenerate all outputs through the established one-way workflow.

Sunday evening plan

Assume a 6:00 PM start. This makes about five portions, depending on the amount of chicken: one Monday hospital meal, two Monday-dinner portions, and two Tuesday portions. If there is anything beyond that, freeze it Sunday night.

6:00–6:10 PM — Set up

- Confirm the refrigerator is 40°F or colder and the freezer is 0°F or colder.
- Set out shallow containers, labels, a food thermometer, and an ice bath or several ice packs.
- Wash hands and keep raw chicken, its board, and utensils separate from the vegetables and cooked food.
- Label containers: “Monday hospital,” “Monday dinner,” “Tuesday,” and “Freeze.”

6:10–6:55 PM — Start the rice and vegetables

- Cook the brown rice according to its package directions. When it is done, do not leave it sitting in the cooking pot; it will cool much faster spread in shallow containers.
- Cut the carrots and broccoli. Toss the carrots and chickpeas with lemon, salt, pepper, and a little oil if available.
- Keep the broccoli separate until later so it does not overcook.

6:25–7:10 PM — Cook the chicken and vegetables

- Heat the oven to 425°F.
- Season the chicken thighs with lemon zest or juice, salt, and pepper. Roast them on a separate lined tray or in a separate section from the vegetables.
- Roast the carrots, chickpeas, and chicken. Add the broccoli for the final 10–15 minutes.
- Check the thickest part of every chicken thigh with a thermometer; remove them only when they reach 165°F. Let them rest briefly, then slice or portion them so they cool quickly.

6:45–7:10 PM — Make the cold sauce

- Mix yogurt with lemon juice or zest and a little salt.
- Keep it separate from the hot food. Do not freeze the yogurt sauce; its texture may split. Use it cold with the Monday and Tuesday portions.

7:10–7:30 PM — Portion for rapid cooling

- Spread the rice in a shallow layer, ideally no more than about 2 inches deep.
- Put chicken and vegetables into shallow, single-meal containers rather than one large casserole.
- Leave lids loosely set or ajar while the food is actively steaming. Do not leave the food on the counter to cool for an extended period.
- Put the containers in the refrigerator with space around them. A shallow container of hot food can be refrigerated directly; avoid putting a deep, hot pot in the refrigerator.
- For the portions marked “Freeze,” place the shallow containers in an ice bath briefly, stirring the rice or vegetables if needed, then transfer them to the freezer once they are no longer hot. Keep the containers spaced apart until frozen.

7:30–8:00 PM — Finish storage

- Check that the food is cooling promptly. As a conservative target, get it below 70°F within two hours of cooking and to 41°F or below within six hours total; faster is better, especially for the rice.
- Once chilled, close the containers tightly.
- Keep the Monday and Tuesday portions refrigerated at 40°F or below. The Sunday-cooked food is within the normal three-to-four-day refrigerated-leftover window through Tuesday.
- Freeze any extra portion that will not be eaten by Tuesday. Label it with the contents and Sunday’s date.

Monday hospital meal

Pack the cold “Monday hospital” container directly from the refrigerator:

- Chicken, rice, broccoli/carrots, and chickpeas in one container.
- Lemon-yogurt sauce in a separate leakproof container.
- Add an ice pack and carry it in an insulated lunch bag.
- Put it in the hospital refrigerator on arrival if one is available. If it cannot stay refrigerated, keep it surrounded by ice packs and eat it promptly rather than leaving it at room temperature for the shift.

At lunch:

- Remove the yogurt sauce and lemon.
- Microwave the chicken, rice, and vegetables covered but vented, stirring the rice and rotating the container halfway through.
- Heat until every part reaches 165°F, checking several spots with a food thermometer if possible. Let it stand briefly, then add the cold yogurt sauce.
- Reheat only the amount being eaten. Do not re-refrigerate a portion that has already been reheated and partly served.

Monday dinner and Tuesday

- Leave Monday dinner portions refrigerated so dinner remains independent of Devika’s arrival time.
- If she arrives late, reheat one portion in the microwave or in a covered pan with a splash of water. Heat to 165°F throughout.
- Take Kibo’s evening walk on the normal schedule rather than waiting for her; around 6:00–6:30 PM is the useful default from your established routine.
- Use any unopened, still-cold Monday portion for Tuesday if needed. Treat Tuesday as the final planned use of the refrigerated batch; freeze anything beyond that now rather than trying to stretch it.

Before bed Sunday

- Put Kibo’s leash and harness by the door.
- Assign Monday’s morning walk before Devika leaves and the evening walk around the normal evening time, with no dependence on her finishing time.
- Put the Monday meal, ice pack, water bottle, badge, phone, and authentication app together by the door.

Safety basis: USDA recommends shallow containers, refrigeration or freezing within two hours, refrigerated leftovers within three to four days, and reheating leftovers to 165°F. FDA cooling guidance uses the stricter two-stage target of 135°F to 70°F within two hours, then to 41°F or below within four additional hours.

Classification: localized tenant-specific queueing/backpressure, not yet a demonstrated scheduler-fairness failure or fleet-wide ingest-edge incident.

The evidence against a broad scheduler failure is:

- Dispatch errors and accepted-point accounting are normal.
- Other tenants are unaffected.
- The tenant is below its eight-request waiting cap.
- There is no current evidence of empty tenants remaining in the round-robin ring.

However, seven queued requests and a 2.6-second queue-wait p99 are enough to investigate before changing anything. Do not raise the cap or alter scheduling yet.

Smallest evidence set

1. Trace a small request sample

For 3–5 affected-tenant requests, plus one request from an unaffected tenant, capture one correlated trace containing:

- Client request start and declared deadline.
- Ingest-edge receive/admission time.
- Waiting-queue enqueue time.
- Tenant-ring insertion and each scheduler turn considered.
- Pod and tenant active counts at each skipped turn.
- Actual permit reservation and dequeue time.
- Decompression/handler start and completion.
- Response-write completion.
- Client cancellation, disconnect, or timeout time and reason.

Use request IDs and a bounded tenant identifier; do not add raw unbounded tenant labels to metrics.

The decisive scheduler fields are: “was the request eligible?”, “was a pod slot available?”, and “did the ring advance past it or contain stale/empty entries?”

2. Check the timeout boundary

For the same traces, compare:

- Client deadline origin: request creation, connection acquisition, or only server submission.
- Client cancellation timestamp.
- Gateway/proxy timeout.
- Ingest-edge server timeout.
- Handler completion timestamp.
- Response-write/reset timestamp.

A client-timeout explanation is supported if the client deadline expires before or near handler/response completion, especially when the request’s actual ingest-edge queue wait is materially smaller than the end-to-end elapsed time. Reproduce once with a controlled client using a longer deadline and connection reuse, without changing ingest-edge.

3. Check queue age against eligibility

For the incident window, retrieve only:

- Affected tenant queue depth.
- Oldest waiting-request age.
- Per-request queue wait for the sampled traces.
- Scheduler dispatch turns and ring contents.
- Pod active count versus the four-active limit.
- Affected-tenant active count versus the two-active limit.
- Any cancellation/removal events.

Interpretation:

- Fairness/work-conservation failure: a live request remains queued while it is eligible, a pod slot is genuinely available, and the scheduler skips it or waits for a later ring rebuild; stale empty tenants or a non-advancing ring appear in the same interval.
- Expected tenant backpressure: the pod is at four active, or the tenant is at two active, or the request is correctly waiting behind eligible work; queue age tracks actual permit occupancy.
- Client-held-open/timeout behavior: requests are canceled or held until the client deadline, while server-side queue/dispatch timing is normal; handler or connection time consumes most of the deadline.
- Cancellation cleanup issue: client cancellations remove the request from the tenant queue but the tenant remains in the ring, or queue depth/ring membership diverges.

Decision: keep ingest-edge unchanged unless the trace proves an eligible request was skipped while capacity was idle, or proves stale empty tenants/ring advancement caused the wait. If queue age is explained by occupied permits or the client’s deadline, remediate the client timeout/connection budget instead.

Ear-care plan today

- Gently wipe only the visible outer flap and entrance with dry gauze or a soft cloth. Do not probe into the canal.

- Take a clear photo of the pink area now and compare it later today and tomorrow. Note the number of scratching episodes and head shakes.

Monitoring window

Contact his regular veterinarian if scratching or head shaking continues beyond 24 hours without improvement, recurs repeatedly, or the pinkness is still present or not clearly better by 48 hours. Do not keep repeatedly cleaning the ear, since over-cleaning can worsen irritation.

Seek veterinary advice promptly—same day or next available appointment—for:

- Increasing frequency or intensity of scratching or head shaking
- Pain, resisting gentle handling, or vocalizing
- Redness spreading into the canal or face
- New swelling of the flap, especially a soft or thickened “puffy” area
- Discharge, blood, excess wax, foul odor, or an obstructed-looking canal
- Persistent rubbing of the ear on furniture or the floor

Seek urgent care if he develops a head tilt, loss of balance, marked lethargy, vomiting associated with ear symptoms, facial weakness, severe pain, active bleeding, or rapidly developing ear-flap swelling.

The smallest useful staging comparison is a one-variable A/B replay:

1. Use two fresh, otherwise identical staging processes/pods.
2. Run the same deterministic replay for 25 minutes with the same route count, input rate, and snapshot cadence.
3. Treatment: normal route-table snapshot serialization.
4. Control: exercise the same snapshot trigger and metadata path, but immediately release/discard the serialized result rather than retaining it in a cache, queue, or generation structure. Do not change routing behavior.
5. Let both processes idle for at least 10 minutes without restarting them. Capture a profile before and after one explicit full GC during the idle period; do not force GC during the replay.

Collect at baseline, every few minutes during replay, at replay stop, and at +1, +6, and +10 minutes idle:

- RSS/working-set memory
- Heap live/in-use bytes after GC
- Heap committed/reserved bytes
- Cumulative allocated bytes and allocation rate
- Allocation/object counts attributed to snapshot serialization and route-table objects
- GC count, CPU, and pause time
- Snapshot count, serialized bytes, duration, and any pending queue/cache/retired-generation count
- Heap profiles at baseline, peak, and idle:
  - allocated/allocation-space profile
  - live/in-use-space profile

Interpretation:

- Retained memory: after idle and full GC, live heap and snapshot-object counts remain materially above baseline, increase across another replay cycle, or are associated with live references such as a cache, queue, or retired route-table generation. RSS will generally remain elevated as well.
- Allocation pressure: allocation rate and GC activity rise during replay, but after traffic stops and GC runs, live heap and snapshot-object counts return to the baseline/control band. The allocation-space profile is large while the in-use-space profile is not.

The existing drop from 2.6 GiB to 1.9 GiB in six minutes already leans toward replay-driven allocation pressure, but the post-GC live-heap profile is the decisive measurement. This requires only bounded staging work and no owner-map or production change.

This proposal introduces a second, temporary source of truth into a workflow that currently depends on one versioned machine-readable package, generated downstream outputs, and a drift check. Anya could raise the following questions herself:

Drift risks

- What exactly is being overridden: the generated platform file, a repository-side configuration layer, or the token package consumed by the application? An override applied after generation may make the repository no longer reproducible from the canonical package.
- Does CI report the override as intentional, or does it whitelist it and conceal the divergence? Either way, the existing drift check must not silently treat a different platform value as clean.
- Could other platforms continue using the canonical value while one platform uses the local value, producing behavioral and visual divergence that is not visible in Figma or the generated package?
- What happens if the canonical token changes during the seven-day window? Reconciliation may become a conflict rather than a simple upstream copy, and the local value could accidentally win, be discarded, or overwrite a newer canonical decision.
- Can the seven-day period be extended, renewed, or restarted by rebasing or copying the override? If so, “temporary” may become a durable platform-specific exception.
- Are references, aliases, themes, modes, and dependent tokens checked, or only the one overridden key? A locally changed primitive can create less obvious downstream differences.
- Is the exception visible in the generated artifact and release review, or can a consumer receive a value that no generated representation records?

Rollback risks

- What is the precise rollback operation: remove the local layer, regenerate from the last canonical package, or revert the application change? Those may produce different results.
- Can a release be rolled back atomically if it contains both a canonical package version and a local override? Rolling back only one could leave the application with a mixed token state.
- What happens when the override expires while the repository is on a branch or release line that has not reconciled it? Expiry should fail closed or produce a clearly actionable failure—not silently fall back to an unexpected value.
- If the canonical package has advanced before rollback, is the system able to restore the exact previously shipped effective value, rather than merely using today’s canonical value?
- Are caches, lockfiles, generated files, build artifacts, and release bundles guaranteed to discard the override during rollback?
- Does a generator failure or partial generation leave the prior published package unchanged, as the current fail-closed workflow requires, or could the exception result in a mixed set of old and new outputs?

Auditability risks

- Is every override recorded with the token path, canonical value, local value, platform, repository and branch, requestor, approver, reason, creation time, expiry time, package version, generator version, and consuming release?
- Can reviewers see the effective value resolution—canonical value plus local override—without reconstructing it from several repositories?
- Is there an immutable, queryable history showing when the override was created, changed, used in a build, reconciled, expired, or removed?
- Does CI fail or alert when an override expires, and is there an owner responsible for reconciliation? An expiry notification alone is weaker than a publication block.
- Can an auditor distinguish an approved temporary exception from an accidental edit to a generated file?
- Does the release record preserve both the canonical source and the override metadata needed to reproduce the shipped result later?

A concise framing she could use is:

“Before accepting a seven-day local override, I need to understand how it remains visible to drift detection, how a release and rollback reproduce the exact effective token set, and how the exception is recorded through reconciliation or expiry. Otherwise the proposal changes the canonical-source contract and creates a platform-specific exception that the current workflow was designed to prevent.”

Classify it as an allocation-pressure optimization, not a leak fix.

The evidence supports that classification:

- Identical replay input and staging conditions produced a 2.0 GiB peak without serialization and 2.55 GiB with it.
- The serialization-enabled process fell to 1.88 GiB after two forced post-replay GCs.
- Retained heap was within 2% of baseline.
- Allocation flame graphs localized temporary growth to snapshot buffers.
- There was no production impact.

That shows transient allocation and GC pressure, not evidence of objects being indefinitely retained. Avoid labeling it “leak fixed”: forced GC is useful evidence, but it does not by itself prove that every retention path is absent. The ticket should say “no leak demonstrated; optimize snapshot serialization allocation/peak memory.”

Suggested owner ticket

Title:
Metrics-router: reduce transient allocation pressure from route-table snapshot serialization

Owner:
Alex, with Wes credited for the bounded staging comparison and evidence collection. Keep the work scoped to metrics-router; no owner-map change or production change is implied.

Problem statement:
With identical staging replay input, enabling route-table snapshot serialization increased peak resident memory from 2.0 GiB to 2.55 GiB. Two post-replay full GCs reduced memory to 1.88 GiB, and retained heap differed from baseline by less than 2%. Allocation profiles attribute the temporary growth to snapshot buffers. Investigate and reduce allocation/GC pressure without changing routing behavior.

Evidence to attach:

1. Reproducibility
   - Replay input identity or checksum.
   - Route count, input rate, snapshot cadence, and replay duration.
   - Exact build/configuration for both runs.
   - Number of runs and whether the result reproduced.

2. Memory measurements
   - Baseline, peak, replay-stop, and post-GC RSS.
   - Live/in-use heap after GC.
   - Heap committed/reserved, if available.
   - The stated values: 2.0 GiB baseline/control, 2.55 GiB serialization peak, 1.88 GiB post-GC, and less than 2% retained-heap delta.

3. Allocation and GC evidence
   - Allocation rate and cumulative allocated bytes.
   - GC count, pause time, and CPU cost.
   - Allocation-space and live/in-use-space profiles.
   - Object counts and sizes for snapshot buffers and route-table objects.
   - Any queue, cache, retired-generation, or pending-snapshot counts.

4. Behavioral safety
   - Route-delivery parity against the control.
   - No dropped points/series, routing errors, replay mismatches, or snapshot failures.
   - Request latency and throughput comparison.
   - Confirmation that the experiment remained staging-only and caused no production change.

Acceptance criteria:

- Reproduce the observed allocation-pressure signature in at least three bounded staging runs, or document why the result cannot be reproduced.
- After replay stops and the prescribed full GC completes, live heap and snapshot-buffer counts return to the agreed baseline band. A reasonable current guardrail is the observed retained-heap delta of less than 2%; tighten it only if the team has a stronger baseline measurement.
- No monotonic increase in post-GC live heap, snapshot-buffer count, pending queue size, cache size, or retired-generation count across repeated replay cycles.
- Reduce the serialization-enabled peak-memory overhead from the observed +0.55 GiB toward an explicitly approved budget. Do not invent the budget in the implementation: derive it from the metrics-router pod limit and required operational headroom. For example, if a 10% peak-over-baseline budget is approved, the target would be no more than 2.2 GiB for this replay.
- Reduce snapshot-related allocation rate and/or GC work without increasing p99 latency, GC pause time, CPU beyond the agreed limits, or snapshot duration.
- Preserve exact routing and snapshot semantics:
  - identical route output,
  - no dropped or duplicated data,
  - no changed publication/retirement behavior,
  - no serialization correctness regressions.
- Add a regression benchmark or test covering replay, snapshot cadence, and post-replay idle/GC behavior.
- Attach before/after profiles and a short comparison table to the ticket.
- Keep the change staging-only until the metrics-router owner reviews the evidence and explicitly approves any production rollout.

The ticket should have a separate non-acceptance note:

“Current results do not establish a memory leak and should not be counted as a leak remediation. Devika is comparing a 12-hour Saturday block with an 8-hour Wednesday swing block. Both are daytime/evening assignments, not overnight coverage; the trade reduces the scheduled workday by four hours but moves the household disruption from the weekend to a late weekday.

Saturday 7:00 AM–7:00 PM

Schedule predictability
- The hours are clear and bounded, but a full Saturday is unavailable.
- It removes one shared weekend day and may also make Friday night feel like preparation rather than free time.
- The weekend loss is concentrated: after the block, Sunday remains available, but Saturday itself cannot be used spontaneously.

Commute spillover
- The commute occurs early Saturday and after 7:00 PM. The exact burden depends on Devika’s travel time and how reliably signout ends on schedule.
- There is less risk of a weekday evening collision, but the long service day means even a nominal 7:00 PM end may produce a late arrival.
- There is no reason to treat 7:00 PM as the home-arrival time; meals and Kibo’s care should not depend on her leaving exactly then.

Recovery
- The 12-hour day is the more physically demanding option.
- Sunday may be partly usable, but it should not automatically be treated as a fully free shared day; Saturday evening and possibly Sunday morning may function as recovery.
- The main recovery advantage is that the following day is not a workday, assuming no other assignment or commitment is scheduled.

Practical home logistics
- Friday evening: place badge, phone, authentication app, water, and other morning essentials by the door.
- Arrange the morning Kibo walk and feeding without relying on Devika having time before a 7:00 AM start.
- Alex handles the Saturday evening walk and Kibo’s dinner on the normal schedule.
- Prepare a reheatable dinner for Devika rather than waiting to eat together or asking her to coordinate from the hospital.
- Keep Saturday night quiet and avoid assuming she will want to socialize or make plans after getting home.
- Protect Sunday from errands or travel until her actual post-block energy is known.

Wednesday 2:00 PM–10:00 PM

Schedule predictability
- The shift preserves the shared weekend, which is the clearest household benefit.
- Wednesday morning remains available, but it should not be filled with demanding plans just because the clinical block starts later.
- The disruption is narrower in hours but extends into the evening and may affect Thursday morning depending on the next day’s schedule.

Commute spillover
- The afternoon departure and late return create the more consequential commute question. The commute may overlap with normal weekday congestion on the way in, and a 10:00 PM end is not the same as arriving home at 10:00 PM.
- Any charting, handoff, discharge work, or delayed signout could push the return later.
- The key fact to confirm is whether 10:00 PM is a genuine hard stop and whether the next day starts early.

Recovery
- The shorter block leaves four fewer scheduled hours and avoids giving up a weekend day.
- It is not an overnight, so it should not create the same sleep inversion as a night block.
- Still, the late return can make Wednesday feel like a full-day disruption: the morning is not entirely free, the evening is unavailable, and Thursday may begin with less recovery than the written schedule suggests.
- Recovery is likely better than after the Saturday block if Thursday is reasonably protected; it may be worse if Thursday begins with an early clinical commitment.

Practical home logistics
- Devika can potentially handle Kibo’s morning walk if that fits her preparation and commute, but the morning should remain low-pressure rather than become a second work period.
- Have lunch or an early meal ready before she leaves; do not assume she will have a normal dinner break at work.
- Alex handles Kibo’s evening walk and dinner independently of Devika’s arrival.
- Leave Devika a simple reheatable meal for when she gets home, with no need for arrival updates.
- Keep Wednesday night quiet and prepare Thursday-morning essentials before bed if the next day starts early.
- Preserve the weekend for the shared time the trade is meant to protect rather than letting the swing simply shift all household plans into recovery.

Neutral comparison

- Best for preserving the weekend: Wednesday swing.
- Best for avoiding a late weekday commute: Saturday block, although Saturday still has a late return after a longer day.
- Shorter and less total work exposure: Wednesday swing.
- Easier next-day recovery: depends mainly on Thursday’s start time; Wednesday is favorable only if Thursday is not an early or heavy assignment.
- Fewer evening household obligations during the workday: neither option eliminates them. Saturday requires coverage across the whole day; Wednesday specifically requires independent coverage of Kibo’s evening walk and dinner.
- More likely to create a “recovery day” afterward: Saturday, because it is a 12-hour weekend service day.
- Main cost of the trade: a late Wednesday commute and lost shared Wednesday dinner/evening.
- Main benefit of the trade: four fewer work hours and preservation of the shared weekend.

The practical decision test is therefore not simply “weekend versus weekday.” It is:

1. Is preserving the weekend worth accepting a late Wednesday return?
2. Does Thursday begin early enough that Wednesday night would materially reduce recovery?
3. Is 10:00 PM a firm end, or can the shift routinely spill later?
4. Can Alex reliably own Kibo’s Wednesday evening walk and dinner without needing Devika to coordinate?
5. Can the Saturday option be absorbed without treating Sunday as a guaranteed fully usable day?

Given the criteria you have been using, Devika’s leaning toward the trade is understandable: it preserves the weekend and reduces the scheduled block by four hours. The unresolved risk is whether the Wednesday late commute and Thursday recovery cost are small enough in practice; that is the specific information worth confirming before Tuesday morning.

Do not use this light for night riding until it passes the sequence below. Because tapping the body reproduces the shutoff, treat it as a likely internal connection, switch, or battery-protection fault—not merely a mounting problem.

Non-destructive diagnostic sequence

1. Safety check
   - Do not open, puncture, pry, crush, heat, or water-test the sealed case.
   - Stop immediately and retire the light if you notice swelling, a split case, unusual heat, chemical smell, hissing, corrosion, or moisture inside the lens.
   - If any of those are present, do not charge it; follow the manufacturer’s battery/e-waste instructions.

2. External inspection
   - Examine the lens, housing seams, button, charging-port cover, and mount interface under good light.
   - Look for cracks, looseness, grit, corrosion, or a button that feels sticky or has excessive travel.
   - Confirm the charging-port cover closes fully and that there is no visible moisture or debris.

3. Charge and document
   - Charge it with the manufacturer-recommended cable and source, on a nonflammable surface and while nearby.
   - Note whether the charge indicator behaves normally and whether the light becomes warm.
   - After charging, disconnect it and verify that it starts normally and retains the selected mode.

4. Remove the mounting variable
   - Test the light off the bicycle, held stationary in your hand or placed on a padded, stable surface.
   - Turn it on and let it run for at least 10–15 minutes.
   - Do not rely on the mount as a heat sink or electrical contact unless the manufacturer specifically designed it that way.

5. Reproduce the fault gently
   - While the light is on, tap each broad housing surface lightly with one fingertip, using roughly the force of ordinary road vibration—not a hard impact.
   - Test near the button, charging-port end, lens, and rear housing separately.
   - If it flickers, changes mode, or shuts off even once, stop testing. That is a confirmed fault.
   - Do not bend the case, shake it aggressively, drop it, or use tools to strike it.

6. Check the control
   - Repeat the test while keeping your finger away from the button.
   - If tapping near the button causes a mode change or shutoff, the button or its internal switch may be failing.
   - If tapping elsewhere causes a shutoff, an internal connection or battery-protection circuit is more likely.

7. Check the mount separately
   - Inspect the clip, adapter, and fastener for cracks or looseness.
   - Reinstall the light and repeat only the stationary run and gentle vibration check.
   - If it fails off the mount, the mount is not the cause. If it works off the mount but fails only when mounted, replace or repair the mount before further evaluation—but do not trust it for night riding until the complete mounted setup remains reliable.

8. Manufacturer remedy
   - Check the manual or manufacturer support page for an approved reset, firmware update, or warranty process.
   - Use only procedures that do not involve opening the sealed battery compartment.

Your response was appropriate: normal shutdown, unplugging the UPS, and not opening it. A repeating “replace battery” alarm with a 2018 battery label is consistent with an end-of-life battery; many UPS manufacturers specify roughly 3–5 years for sealed lead-acid UPS batteries.[2] Treat the UPS as battery-powered even while unplugged.

1. Safe storage now

- Leave the UPS unplugged and disconnected from all equipment.
- Keep it upright in a cool, dry, well-ventilated place on a stable, nonconductive surface, away from heat, sunlight, flames, metal clutter, and combustible materials.
- Do not place it in an airtight box or seal over any battery vents. Sealed lead-acid batteries can still vent hydrogen under abnormal charging or fault conditions.[6]
- Do not recharge or test it merely to silence the alarm. If it must be retained briefly for model identification, handle it only externally and inspect it periodically without opening it.
- Because the battery is already old, do not plan extended storage with the battery installed. Arrange replacement or recycling instead. Long-term storage reduces battery life and requires periodic manufacturer-specified recharging; APC, for example, recommends charging at least every six months under moderate storage temperatures.[4]

2. Model check before buying anything

Record or photograph—without opening the case:

- Manufacturer and exact UPS model number
- Serial number
- Input/output voltage
- Any “replace battery,” “battery pack,” or part number printed on the exterior
- Battery chemistry printed on the label, such as SLA, VRLA, AGM, or lead-acid
- Battery voltage and amp-hour rating, if visible

The model number is commonly on a label on the rear, underside, or side rather than the front.[3] Use the manufacturer’s battery selector and the manual for the exact model. Do not select a replacement solely by matching the old battery’s physical size, voltage, connector, or label. The correct pack may include a specific number of cells, wiring, fuse, tray, connector, or battery-management arrangement. Eaton’s guidance, for example, requires the same type and number of batteries or battery packs and recommends manufacturer-supplied replacements.[5]

3. User-replaceable sealed battery versus internally sealed UPS

“Sealed” normally describes the battery chemistry—it does not mean every UPS may be opened by the user.

User-replaceable sealed battery or cartridge:

- Replace it yourself only if the exact manual explicitly provides a user-replacement procedure.
- Use the exact approved cartridge or an explicitly compatible replacement with the same type, number, voltage, capacity, connectors, and protection.
- Follow the manual’s shutdown sequence. Unplug AC, disconnect all loads, and wait as directed.
- Remove watches, rings, bracelets, and other metal jewelry; use insulated-handled tools and avoid shorting the terminals. UPS batteries can deliver very high short-circuit current and cause burns or electric shock.[5]
- Do not open, puncture, cut, crush, refill, solder, or dismantle the sealed cells. Replace the complete cartridge or approved battery assembly.
- If the case is cracked, swollen, leaking, hot, or smells abnormal, do not remove it yourself. Contact the manufacturer, an authorized service provider, or your local hazardous-waste authority for handling instructions.

Internally sealed or non-user-serviceable UPS:

- Do not remove the UPS cover or attempt to reach the battery, even though the unit is unplugged. Internal capacitors and the battery can retain hazardous energy.
- Treat “no user-serviceable parts” or the absence of a documented replacement procedure as a service requirement.
- Have the manufacturer or qualified service personnel replace the battery, or replace the entire UPS.
- Some larger UPS models require additional isolation procedures beyond simply unplugging the cord. Manufacturer manuals specifically warn that certain units have no user-serviceable internal parts.[5]

4. Replacement and testing

Once the exact model and procedure are confirmed:

- Replace the battery promptly rather than continuing to use the UPS with the alarm active.
- Do not assume the UPS itself is healthy just because a new battery fits. After replacement, follow the manual’s charging, self-test, and runtime-test procedure.
- If the UPS continues alarming, becomes hot, emits an odor, shows an internal fault, or fails its self-test, stop using it and have the UPS serviced or replaced.
- If the UPS is several years old, compare the cost and age of the unit with a new, safety-certified UPS. A replacement battery does not correct a failed charger, inverter, surge component, or thermal fault.

5. Disposal

For a normal, intact sealed lead-acid UPS battery:

- Do not put it in household trash or curbside recycling.
- Return it to the battery retailer, the UPS manufacturer’s take-back program, a battery recycler, or a local household hazardous-waste facility. EPA identifies small sealed lead-acid batteries as commonly used in UPS equipment and recommends retailer or household-hazardous-waste recycling.[1]
- Keep the battery upright and protect exposed terminals from short circuits with nonconductive terminal covers or tape, as appropriate for the recycler’s instructions.
- Do not transport a damaged, hot, swollen, or leaking battery until the receiving facility tells you how to do so.
- Do not ship it casually. Use the manufacturer’s prepaid recycling packaging or follow the carrier and recycler’s instructions for sealed lead-acid batteries.

If the UPS or battery is marked lithium-ion rather than lead-acid, stop and use lithium-battery hazardous-waste guidance instead. Do not assume the handling or disposal route is the same.[7]

6. Signs requiring urgent isolation

Stop handling it and keep people away if you notice any of the following:

- Heat, rapid temperature rise, bulging, swelling, deformation, or a cracked case
- Sulfur/acid, solvent, or burning-electrical odor
- Hissing, popping, smoke, vapor, sparks, arcing, or discoloration
- Visible liquid, crystals, corrosion, or leakage
- The UPS or battery starts smoking, ignites, or becomes violently hot
- A lithium-ion label combined with swelling, odor, smoke, or unusual noise

If there is smoke, fire, intense heat, or rapidly worsening behavior, evacuate, close the room door if safe, call emergency services, and do not move or open the UPS. Do not attempt to fight a battery fire or carry a hot/damaged battery outside. Damaged lithium-ion batteries can produce rapidly spreading fires and toxic gases.[7]

For acid or electrolyte exposure, immediately flush skin or eyes with running water for at least 15 minutes and seek medical attention; do not open the battery to investigate.[6]

Sources:
[1] https://www.epa.gov/recycle/used-household-batteries
[2] https://www.apc.com/us/en/faqs/FA156520
[3] https://www.apc.com/us/en/tools/ups_replacement_battery_selector
[4] https://apc.com/us/en/faqs/FA156516
[5] https://www.eaton.com/content/dam/eaton/products/backup-power-ups-surge-it-power-distribution/backup-power-ups/eaton-5sc-ups/eaton-5sc-ups-user-manual-northamerica.pdf
[6] https://data.energizer.com/pdfs/leadacid_psds.pdf
[7] https://lafd.org/lithiumion-battery-safety

A symptom-free reassessment is permission to follow the progression—not permission to skip it. Since the new moderate circuit is undercling-heavy, skip that circuit today.

60-minute bounded session

0–5 minutes: readiness check

- Confirm ordinary use, wrist/finger motion, and light grip are pain-free.
- Do a few relaxed wrist circles, open/close the hands, and gentle forearm rotations.
- If the familiar forearm ache is present at rest or during this check, do not climb.

5–15 minutes: longer forearm warm-up

Keep everything easy and below fatigue:

- 2–3 minutes of general movement.
- 10–15 relaxed wrist-flexion and wrist-extension repetitions.
- 10–15 gentle pronation/supination repetitions per side.
- Several slow, pain-free hand opens and closes.
- Very light open-hand contact on large holds or a jug: 2–3 brief sets of 10–15 seconds, with full relaxation between sets.
- No loaded undercling position, crimping, pinching, hard squeezing, or testing the previously provocative movement.

The forearm should still feel quiet—not merely “looser”—before climbing.

15–30 minutes: easy climbing and footwork

Use:

- Easy open-hand slabs.
- Easy vertical footwork problems.
- Low traverses.
- Large, positive holds that can be held with a relaxed open hand.

Rules:

- Stay well below normal difficulty; choose problems you could complete without gripping hard.
- Focus on quiet feet, straight-forward body positions, and relaxed hands.
- Downclimb whenever practical; avoid jumping down.
- Take 1–2 minutes between attempts.
- Stop a problem rather than squeezing harder to finish it.

30–45 minutes: controlled progression

Continue only if the first climbing block was completely symptom-free.

Choose one progression variable only:

- Slightly more time on the wall, or
- One modestly harder easy problem, or
- A few additional low traverses.

Do not increase difficulty and volume together. Keep the terrain slab/vertical and keep every hold open-hand and low effort. Cap each problem at two attempts; fatigue must not turn a relaxed grip into hard gripping.

45–50 minutes: conservative final exposure

Only if the forearm remains entirely quiet:

- Do 1–2 more easy problems or low traverses at the same intensity.
- Do not use this block to “see what happens” on underclings.
- If the available options require pulling hard, crimping, pinching, or underclinging, end the climbing portion early.

50–55 minutes: cooldown

- Easy walking.
- Gentle wrist and forearm range of motion.
- Relaxed hand opening/closing.
- No stretching into pain and no final grip test.

55–60 minutes: reassessment and log

Record:

- Symptoms during each block, using 0–10.
- Whether any symptom was familiar, sharp, escalating, or grip-limiting.
- Whether symptoms settled promptly after stopping.
- Any change in wrist/finger motion or ordinary grip.

Stop criteria

Stop the current problem immediately for:

- Any recognizable return of the forearm ache, especially in the familiar flexor area.
- Sharp, escalating, or persistent pain.
- Pain that changes your grip, wrist position, movement, or confidence.
- Weakness, slipping, loss of ordinary grip, numbness, or tingling.
- Needing to squeeze harder to compensate for fatigue.

End the session—not just the problem—if symptoms recur after rest, reach 1–2/10 and do not promptly settle, or appear on a second easy attempt. Do not continue because the symptom fades between attempts.

Progression rule

Today passes only if the session stays symptom-free, ordinary use remains normal afterward, and there is no increase in symptoms later today or tomorrow morning. If that is clean, repeat this same level before adding another variable. Keep loaded underclings, hard gripping, and the moderate undercling-heavy circuit excluded until they are specifically reintroduced through the prescribed progression or cleared by the clinician.

Kings County jury-service checklist for Monday

Your summons controls the required date, 8:30 AM report time, location, and availability through 5:00 PM. The official Kings County page identifies the Jury Division at 360 Adams Street, Room 156, and points jurors to the Kings daily call-in information, but verify that your summons does not direct you to another courthouse or room.[1][2]

Evening before

Verify from the summons or official court site

- Confirm the service date and the exact required report time: 8:30 AM.
- Confirm the exact courthouse, street address, entrance, courtroom or room, and whether you must report in person or first use a standby/call-in message.
- Check whether there is a Sunday evening or Monday morning call-in/reporting instruction. The official Kings County page says daily call-in information is available through the Kings juror site.[1]
- Review any stated requirements for:
  - Summons or questionnaire
  - Government-issued photo ID
  - Juror/index number
  - Forms or proof
  - Phones, laptops, cameras, bags, food, or other items subject to courthouse security
- Check the court’s current security or entry guidance rather than assuming that ordinary items are permitted.
- Note the correct contact procedure if illness, an emergency, or a transportation problem will prevent timely attendance. The official page says that jurors who have not yet been selected or sworn should call the number for the building where they are serving, and should not email while serving.[1]
- If you are already seeking a postponement or excusal, do not wait until Monday; the Kings County page says postponement applications must be submitted before the service date.[1]

Ordinary preparation

- Put the summons and photo ID together where you will not forget them.
- Charge your phone fully and pack a charger or power bank only if permitted by the courthouse rules.
- Turn work notifications off and set a work status or automatic reply if needed. You do not need to notify the court merely because work notifications are disabled.
- Set out weather-appropriate, comfortable clothing and shoes.
- Prepare water, food, medication, and reading material only after checking the courthouse’s current rules.
- Confirm your route and any transit alternatives.
- Keep the 7:20 AM departure plan. A 55-minute trip puts the estimated arrival at about 8:15 AM, leaving roughly 15 minutes before the required 8:30 AM report time for entry. If courthouse security or transit conditions may take longer, leave earlier rather than relying on the estimate.

Morning of service

Before leaving

- Check the summons again for the address, room, report time, and any special instruction.
- Check the official Kings reporting/call-in information if your summons directs you to do so.
- Confirm that your phone, summons, photo ID, and any expressly required documents are with you.
- Keep work notifications off, but leave the phone available for personal, court, and emergency calls.
- Leave at 7:20 AM, or earlier if the route or entry conditions make the 15-minute post-arrival buffer inadequate.

At the courthouse

- Follow the summons and courthouse staff instructions over assumptions or general preparation advice.
- Report to the specified location and remain available through 5:00 PM unless court personnel release you or give different instructions.
- Do not use work messaging or handle work tasks while serving unless an actual emergency requires it.

When to communicate

No court communication is needed if:

- You are still able to report at 8:30 AM.
- You can remain available through 5:00 PM.
- You have simply turned off work notifications.
- Your route, preparation, or plans are unchanged.

Contact the court only if your ability to comply actually changes—for example, illness, an emergency, a delay that will prevent timely reporting, or a situation that means you can no longer remain available through 5:00 PM.

If that happens:

- Use the contact method and number specified on the summons.
- If you have not yet been selected or sworn, call the number for the courthouse where you are serving. The official Kings County page lists:
  - 360 Adams Street: 347-404-9856
  - 320 Jay Street: 347-404-9850
  - 141 Livingston Street: 347-404-9882
  - 120 Schermerhorn Street: 347-404-9882[1]
- Do not rely on email for a same-day serving-juror problem; the official page specifically says not to email if you are serving as a juror.[1]
- State only the operational facts: your name and juror/index number, courthouse, summons date, what changed, whether you are delayed or unable to attend, and the best callback number.
- Follow the instructions you receive and document the time, office, and person or voicemail reached.
- If you are sworn as a grand juror, use the wardens’ contact procedure instead of the trial-juror numbers.[1]

Sources:

[1] https://www.nycourts.gov/courts/2nd-judicial-district/kings-county-clerks-office/jury-service — Kings County Jury Service | New York Courts

[2] https://www.nycourts.gov/courts/2nd-judicial-district/kings-county-jury — Kings County Jury | New York Courts
