Good call keeping Kibo out of it. Fuzzing near a reinforced D-ring can be more than cosmetic even when the webbing and stitching look intact; don’t load-test it. Inspect under bright light for broken strands, thinning, spreading, or any D-ring movement, but given its location, replacement is the safest choice if there’s any uncertainty.

Assuming you mean Kibo’s leash webbing and stitching:

Safety-focused inspection checklist

1. Prepare safely
- Inspect in bright light with the leash unloaded and clean enough to see the fibers.
- Examine both sides and the full length: especially the clasp loop, handle attachment, folds, bartacks, box-X stitching, and areas rubbing on hardware.
- Do not attach it to Kibo or use a pull, jerk, hanging weight, or “strength test.”

2. Apply only light hand tension
- Hold the webbing in line with itself and gently remove the slack—just enough to flatten it.
- Do not yank, shock-load, twist, side-load the clasp, or pull hard enough to stretch the material.
- While lightly tensioned, check whether any cut, gap, thinning, or stitch separation opens or changes shape. If it moves or spreads, stop.

3. Superficial fuzzing — potentially cosmetic only
Fuzzing may be superficial when all of the following are true:
- Fibers are merely raised or pill-like on the surface.
- The webbing remains its original width, thickness, flexibility, and flat shape.
- No individual load-bearing strands are cut or missing.
- There is no hole, slit, edge notch, longitudinal tear, narrowing, or visibly thinned patch.
- Light tension does not open the area or reveal a gap.
- The fuzzing is away from attachment folds and load-bearing stitching.
- Stitch rows remain dense, even, and firmly seated.

Even then, treat it as a reason for more frequent inspection—not as proof that the leash is sound.

4. Compromised webbing — retire immediately
Replace the leash if you see any of these:
- Any visibly cut, severed, or missing webbing fibers.
- A frayed patch that exposes deeper fibers or creates a thin spot.
- A slit, hole, tear, edge cut, scalloping, or narrowing.
- Local stretching, distortion, stiffness, brittleness, glazing, melting, or chemical discoloration.
- Damage at the handle, clasp loop, folded attachment, or any other load-bearing point.
- The damage opens, gaps, shifts, or becomes more visible under light hand tension.
- Uncertain damage that you cannot confidently classify as surface-only.

A small damaged patch still counts: the previously noted roughly 1 cm area with visibly cut fibers near the handle was a replacement threshold, even though the stitching had remained intact.

5. Inspect load-bearing stitching separately
Retire the leash if any load-bearing stitch:
- Is broken, missing, or visibly skipped.
- Has pulled loops, spreading rows, or a gap between the folded layers.
- Shows thread being pulled out of the webbing.
- Has loosened enough that the fold or attachment can shift under light tension.
- Is cut, abraded through, heat-damaged, or separating at the handle or clasp loop.

Cosmetic fuzz on thread may be less serious if the stitch pattern is still dense, continuous, and firmly seated, but do not dismiss:
- A loose or missing section in a bartack or box-X pattern.
- Stitching that looks intact but allows the folded webbing to open.
- Any uncertainty at the handle or clasp attachment.

6. Check the other failure points
- Clasp closes fully and consistently on its own; no gap, sticking, deformation, or intermittent locking.
- Hardware does not rotate or pull away from the webbing unexpectedly.
- Webbing is fully seated through the clasp attachment.
- Harness attachment ring and front-clip harness remain undamaged and correctly fitted.

Replacement rule

Do not use the leash if there is any cut or missing webbing fiber, local thinning, damage at a load-bearing fold, or any failed/loosening load-bearing stitch. Do not trim, tape, melt, sew, or test it under tension as a repair. Mark it “DO NOT USE” and replace it; when uncertain, choose replacement over continued use.

You did the right thing by unplugging the blender and stopping use. The absence of heat, odor, smoke, moisture, or visible damage is reassuring, but a GFCI that will not latch still needs to be treated as a fault.

Safe, non-destructive isolation sequence:

1. Keep the blender unplugged. Do not plug anything else into the affected receptacle. Keep hands, the floor, and the panel dry.
2. Make only an external check:
   - Look at the GFCI face, plug, cord, and nearby counter/sink area.
   - Stop immediately if you find warmth, buzzing, crackling, discoloration, moisture, a loose receptacle, damaged insulation, or a hot plug.
   - Do not remove the cover, use a meter, tighten wiring, or replace the receptacle.
3. Check for another accessible upstream GFCI. Look at other kitchen receptacles and, if applicable, nearby bathroom, utility, garage, or exterior GFCIs. Without opening anything, press RESET once on any that appears tripped, provided it is dry and shows no warning signs.
   - Return to the kitchen GFCI and press RESET once.
   - If either GFCI trips again or will not latch, stop resetting.
4. Check the electrical panel visually. If it is dry and accessible, identify the kitchen breaker from its label. With the blender unplugged and other loads off:
   - If the handle is visibly between ON and OFF, move it fully OFF, then ON once.
   - If it is not visibly tripped, one deliberate OFF-then-ON reset is still reasonable only if you can confidently identify the kitchen breaker and there are no panel warning signs.
   - Do not cycle it repeatedly. If it trips, will not stay on, or you hear or smell anything unusual, leave it OFF.
5. Try the kitchen GFCI RESET one final time. Do not force the button or keep pressing it if it will not latch.

Do not test the blender again at another receptacle until it has been inspected or tested by someone qualified. A GFCI trip can indicate leakage from the appliance, a receptacle/GFCI failure, wiring trouble, or—if the device is a combination unit—an overcurrent condition. It is not safe to assume that the absence of a visibly tripped breaker rules those out.

Leave the circuit off or unused and request South Slope management service or a licensed electrician if any of these applies:

- The kitchen GFCI will not reset after the upstream-GFCI and one-breaker-reset sequence.
- It trips with nothing plugged in.
- It trips again after a reset.
- The breaker trips, will not stay on, or another outlet or light unexpectedly loses power.
- You see or hear heat, buzzing, crackling, sparks, smoke, burning odor, discoloration, moisture, a loose receptacle, or a hot plug.
- The problem recurs with any appliance, or the blender’s cord, plug, housing, or inlet shows damage.

Given that it currently will not reset even with the blender unplugged, the conservative endpoint is already to leave that receptacle unused and report it for qualified inspection. If you can confidently identify the branch breaker, leave it OFF pending service; otherwise leave the GFCI and receptacle unused rather than switching off an unknown breaker. Smoke, active sparking, or a burning smell warrants moving away from the area and using emergency services for an immediate fire hazard.

The boundary should be:

Semantic pass/fail check

Canonicalize only the comparison representation:

- Parse JSON strictly, rejecting duplicate keys and malformed input.
- Ignore object-key order and insignificant whitespace/newline differences.
- Compare the complete typed structure, including all expected files and fields.
- Keep string versus number, null versus missing, values, field additions/removals/renames, and unknown fields significant.
- Preserve array order unless the schema explicitly defines that particular array as unordered.

Thus, the current North Pier case—same token names and values, differing only in key order and CRLF/LF—should pass the semantic drift check. It should not be reported as token-content drift.

Byte-level boundary

Raw bytes should still matter for deterministic-generation and packaging checks. The generator should aim to emit stable canonical bytes, so repeated runs from the same pinned inputs should be byte-identical. If the semantic comparison passes but bytes differ, classify that separately as a canonical-output or reproducibility issue. Depending on North Pier’s gate policy, it may still block publication, but it must not be described as a token-value mismatch.

Evidence to retain

Do not replace or normalize away the originals. Keep:

- The exact versioned canonical token package used as input.
- The exact generated files as emitted, including their original ordering, whitespace, and line endings.
- The committed/reference artifacts used for comparison.
- The complete file manifest and raw-byte hashes.
- The canonicalized comparison form or semantic diff.
- Generator version, runtime, configuration, dependency lockfile, and relevant stdout/stderr.
- The staging-directory result and publication decision.

That preserves the distinction between “the token data changed,” “the generator emitted noncanonical bytes,” and “the archive/package was not reproducible.” The check remains fail-closed, but the evidence explains which boundary failed. The candidate fix is unsafe: trimming every string value converts a real token change—`" 12 px"` to `"12 px"`—into a false match. Remove value trimming.

Keep the normalization limited to representation-level differences:

- Parse both artifacts with duplicate-key rejection.
- Sort object keys for comparison.
- Normalize CRLF to LF where line endings are non-semantic.
- Preserve string contents exactly, including leading/trailing whitespace.
- Treat additions, removals, type changes, array changes, and any string-value change as drift.

That fixture should be a negative test: the checker must report drift and block publication. If some schema fields genuinely permit surrounding whitespace, define an explicit field-level rule rather than globally trimming all strings.

For semantic comparison, separate three concerns:

1. Raw artifact fidelity
   - Preserve the exact bytes produced by the generator.
   - Keep byte hashes and deterministic-output checks separate from semantic comparison.
   - A formatting-only difference may be harmless semantically but still indicate a noncanonical or nondeterministic generator output.

2. Schema-defined semantic comparison
   Safe normalization is limited to differences the format or schema already declares insignificant, such as:
   - JSON indentation, line endings, and other parser-level whitespace.
   - Object-key ordering.
   - Equivalent escape spellings after parsing, such as a character represented directly versus with a Unicode escape.
   - Array ordering only where the schema explicitly defines the array as an unordered set.
   - Numeric representation only where the schema defines the field as numeric and treats equivalent numeric values alike.

   The comparison should still distinguish strings from numbers, missing fields from `null`, and added, removed, renamed, malformed, or unknown fields. Duplicate keys should be rejected rather than resolved by parser “last key wins” behavior.

3. Canonical-output enforcement
   - Engineering can require generated files to use stable ordering, formatting, escaping, newline, and number rules.
   - That is a reproducibility/output-quality check, not permission to normalize away semantic drift during comparison.

Token-value whitespace must not be silently trimmed, collapsed, or otherwise normalized unless the schema explicitly defines that value as whitespace-insensitive. `"prod"` and `"prod "` may look equivalent to a person, but they are different strings; trimming can convert malformed input into valid input, hide a producer defect, create collisions, or change an identifier/value that consumers treat literally. The same caution applies to case folding, Unicode normalization, punctuation removal, and alias substitution: each requires an explicit schema rule. For example, a schema may permit mixed-case environment names to normalize to lowercase while still rejecting `Prod ` as malformed.

The evidence should preserve both sides of the decision:

- The original canonical source package, including exact bytes and its hash.
- Every generated artifact exactly as emitted, including failed or noncanonical staging output where retention policy permits.
- Input and output manifests, file lists, sizes, and hashes.
- The schema and normalization-policy version used for the comparison.
- The parsed semantic representation or a reproducible canonical comparison representation.
- A structured diff showing whether the difference was formatting, ordering, type, value, structure, or invalid input.
- Generator version, configuration, dependency/lockfile versions, and relevant environment metadata.
- Validation, duplicate-key, collision, and publication-gate diagnostics.

That keeps the boundary clear: design can define token meaning and which fields or values are semantically insensitive; engineering owns parsing, validation, deterministic generation, comparison, evidence, and publication safety.

A practical 15-minute substitute that keeps the longer forearm warmup and gradual loading:

0:00–2:00 — General floor mobility
- Brisk walking or easy marching for 60 seconds.
- Shoulder rolls, arm swings, and gentle thoracic rotations.
- Keep everything comfortable and relaxed; no aggressive stretching.

2:00–5:00 — Forearm and wrist mobility
- 8–10 slow wrist circles each direction.
- 10 gentle pronation/supination reps with elbows at your sides.
- 10 slow open-hand-to-relaxed-fist repetitions.
- 5–8 gentle wrist flexion/extension movements, stopping short of a stretch that feels provocative.

5:00–8:00 — Easy traversing
- Use the easiest available vertical/slab section.
- Do two relaxed traverses of about 60–75 seconds, with 30–45 seconds of rest.
- Keep feet quiet, move slowly, and use large holds with an open hand. No dynamic moves or hard squeezing yet.

8:00–11:00 — Lowest available open-hand route
- Climb the easiest route you can find at roughly 50–60% effort.
- Use open-hand contact and deliberate, controlled movement.
- Downclimb if convenient; otherwise take a full 60–90 seconds before the next attempt.

11:00–15:00 — Second easy route and gradual loading
- Repeat the same route, or choose one small step harder if the first attempt was symptom-free.
- Stay around 60–70% effort, using the most relaxed grip that works.
- Finish with easy shaking-out and forearm relaxation rather than a hard final move.

First-attempt progression after the substitute

1. Lowest-grade vertical/slab route: easy, open-hand, 50–60% effort.
2. Rest 2–3 minutes; repeat the same route or go one small grade step higher at 60–70%.
3. Rest again; choose one modest new demand—slightly steeper terrain, a few underclings, or firmer gripping—but not a max-effort attempt and not all new demands at once.
4. If those are clean during the session and afterward, continue ordinary bouldering without a move cap, increasing only one variable at a time: grade, steepness, grip intensity, or total attempts.

Use your established step-back rule: if pain goes above 2/10, symptoms last 30 minutes, or symptoms appear the next morning, step back and contact the clinician.

Design-validation verdict: do not accept the above-forecast replay evidence until the candidate has these regressions. This is a validation gate only; it is not production authorization.

1. Concurrency and admission linearization

Required regressions:

- Concurrent submitters cannot exceed the global pending bound of 2,048 or the per-tenant bound of 64.
- Tenant and global reservations have one unambiguous admission linearization point.
- The intended sequence is: reserve tenant capacity, reserve global capacity, roll back the tenant reservation if global reservation fails, enqueue, and mark accepted only after both reservations and enqueue succeed.
- Enqueue versus dequeue, cancellation, and simultaneous slot release cannot over-admit or strand capacity.
- A request cannot hold both a pending slot and an active/processing slot in a way that defeats either bound.
- Global-full, tenant-full, and any downstream admission rejection remain distinct outcomes and metrics.
- Repeated concurrent stress runs must leave all counters consistent with the request ledger; no negative counts, over-release, or unexplained residual reservations.

2. Cancellation and terminal-state races

Cover cancellation:

- before tenant reservation;
- after tenant reservation but before global reservation;
- after both reservations but before enqueue;
- after enqueue but before acceptance;
- concurrently with enqueue/acceptance;
- after acceptance during processing;
- concurrently with successful completion, failure, timeout, and retry handling;
- repeated or duplicate cancellation notifications.

The required invariant is exactly one terminal outcome per request. A cancellation that wins before acceptance must produce no accepted contribution. If acceptance wins, cancellation must follow the accepted-request terminal path rather than creating a second outcome or suppressing the original accounting event.

Every path must prove:

- no canceled request is processed or acknowledged as accepted;
- no reservation is leaked;
- no reservation is released twice;
- a reservation that was never acquired is never released;
- the request ledger and capacity counters return to their pre-test values.

3. Slot release and recovery

Required regressions:

- Tenant and global slots are released at the defined lifecycle boundary, not opportunistically or only after unrelated downstream work completes.
- Releases are guarded so each held reservation is returned exactly once on success, failure, timeout, and cancellation.
- A failed global reservation immediately returns the tenant reservation.
- Enqueue failure, cancellation during enqueue, and terminal cleanup all restore capacity one-for-one.
- Releasing one, several, and all available slots wakes blocked admission without waiting for a periodic poll or unrelated traffic.
- A full-capacity condition clears automatically; there must be no stale “full” state, lost wakeup, deadlock, or capacity that requires a manual reset.
- After a cancellation storm, a new request must be able to consume every slot that the canceled work actually released.

4. Noisy-tenant fairness

A per-tenant cap of 64 is necessary but does not establish fairness. The replay must include a continuously flooded tenant alongside low-volume tenants and show:

- the noisy tenant cannot consume more than its 64 pending slots;
- other tenants can use remaining global capacity;
- a newly eligible low-volume tenant is admitted and serviced without waiting for unrelated queue activity or a periodic rebuild;
- the noisy tenant cannot monopolize dispatch or create unbounded queue age for other tenants;
- tenants at an active/concurrency limit are skipped rather than blocking eligible tenants;
- empty or fully canceled tenants leave no stale queue or scheduler membership;
- low-volume tenants receive service within a declared bounded-turn or queue-age criterion;
- per-tenant queue age, pending depth, rejection reason, dispatch/acceptance order, and idle eligible capacity are captured.

The evidence must show work conservation: an eligible request must not wait while capacity is available. Aggregate throughput or a healthy global queue depth is not sufficient.

5. Acceptance and accounting

The replay must use request-level authoritative records, not inferred averages. Required regressions:

- Pre-acceptance rejection contributes zero accepted requests and zero accepted points.
- A request is counted as accepted only after the candidate’s stated acceptance point—both reservations held and enqueue completed.
- Every accepted request contributes exactly once to accepted accounting.
- Every request has exactly one terminal outcome, correlated by request identifier.
- Cancellation against dispatch and cancellation against completion cannot produce both accepted and canceled outcomes, duplicate acceptance, or missing terminal accounting.
- Accepted points equal the exact points represented by accepted requests; do not estimate refused points as refused-request-count multiplied by an average batch size.
- Rejected, canceled-before-acceptance, failed, accepted, and terminally canceled work are separately represented.
- The final ledger must reconcile submitted, pre-acceptance rejected, accepted, terminal outcomes, and exact point totals with zero unexplained gap, drop, or duplicate.
- No points are written downstream after a cancellation that won the acceptance race.
- If the caller’s acceptance-to-terminal budget is part of the September 5 contract, include a regression where queue delay consumes that budget and verify a single cancellation-safe terminal result rather than an ambiguous timeout/retry path.

Acceptance gate for the scheduled replay:

Accept the load evidence only if the run includes the above-forecast/noisy-tenant workload, cancellation races, simultaneous release-and-submit races, recovery-after-saturation, and a request-level accounting reconciliation with zero unexplained discrepancy. Otherwise classify the evidence as insufficient design validation, not as evidence supporting the scheduled replay.

You can remain Infra primary for now. Mild injection-site soreness alone is common and usually settles within 1–2 days or a few days.[1][2][4]

Same-day guidance:

- Arm movement: Use the arm normally and move it gently through comfortable ranges periodically; don’t immobilize it. Routine movement is reasonable, but scale back heavy lifting or strenuous upper-body work if it clearly increases pain.
- Hydration: Drink normally—water with meals and when thirsty. There is no need to force excessive fluids or use special electrolyte products.
- Ordinary activity: Continue normal work, walking, eating, and household activity if you feel well. Rest if fatigue, aches, headache, or fever develops. If you take an over-the-counter pain reliever, use only one you normally can take and follow its label or your clinician’s advice.
- On-call: No coverage change is needed just for mild soreness. Step away from on-call and contact a clinician promptly for a high or persistent fever, rapidly worsening symptoms, severe or unusual weakness, new numbness, difficulty walking, paralysis, or symptoms that concern you. Mild soreness, a low-grade temperature, body aches, headache, or fatigue can occur after the shot, but should generally improve rather than progressively worsen.[1][2][5]

Accepted-Batch Evidence Specification — Mosaic

Purpose

Close the evidence gap identified in the October 15 incident-practice session. The specification defines the minimum durable evidence needed to determine whether an accepted batch was delivered, terminally failed, or lost. It does not authorize another production window, change queue controls, change the owner map, or close the Mosaic scale-response cycle.

Bounded requirements

1. Acceptance-scoped identity
   - At the acceptance boundary, assign one immutable logical identity to each accepted batch, at minimum:
     (tenant_id, accepted_batch_id)
   - Associate the identity with an immutable request fingerprint or equivalent content/range identity.
   - The accepted-batch identity must not change for retries, requeues, worker changes, restarts, or transport failures.

2. Transport-attempt identity
   - Assign a distinct immutable transport_attempt_id to every transport attempt.
   - Persist the link:
     accepted_batch_id → one or more transport_attempt_id values.
   - A retry or requeue creates a new transport attempt; it must never create a new accepted batch or reuse an earlier attempt identity.

3. Exactly one terminal result
   - Persist exactly one authoritative terminal record for every accepted batch.
   - The terminal record must identify the accepted batch, its final state, and the evidence source or commit reference supporting that state.
   - Duplicate, delayed, or reordered callbacks must not create, replace, or obscure a second terminal result.
   - An accepted batch may not remain indefinitely unclassified as “attempted” or “in flight” without an explicit bounded investigation state and reconciliation path.

4. Acceptance population boundary
   - The accepted-batch population begins only after acceptance is durably recorded.
   - Pre-acceptance refusals, including retryable queue-full responses, must be excluded from accepted-batch totals and reconciled separately as refusals.
   - A refused request must not receive an accepted-batch terminal state unless it later crosses the acceptance boundary.

5. Diagnostic exposure
   - Keep raw accepted-batch and transport-attempt identities out of metric labels.
   - Aggregate metrics may expose bounded dimensions such as outcome, stage, and refusal class.
   - Provide a permissioned diagnostic or audit view that can retrieve the accepted-batch identity, linked attempts, terminal result, timestamps, and relevant commit/receipt references.
   - Diagnostic access must be auditable and must not alter queue state or terminal accounting.

6. Reconciliation evidence
   For a defined interval, the evidence package must support an independent reconciliation of:
   - durably accepted batches;
   - linked transport attempts;
   - exactly one terminal result per accepted batch;
   - downstream durable receipt or commit evidence for successful outcomes;
   - explicit terminal failure evidence for unsuccessful outcomes; and
   - pre-acceptance refusals, reported separately.

   The reconciliation must identify any accepted batch with no terminal result, conflicting terminal results, an attempt chain that cannot be followed, or no downstream receipt/explicit failure evidence. Those cases remain unknown or potentially lost; aggregate “no accepted points lost” totals are insufficient.

Ownership and evidence gate

- Wes: implement the identity and terminal-accounting path, preserve identity across retry/requeue, and provide replay, restart, duplicate-callback, and concurrent-race evidence.
- Nadia: define the refusal/accepted population boundary, diagnostic permissions, aggregate-label constraints, and alert/reconciliation semantics.
- The existing queue limits, backpressure behavior, stop conditions, and formal owner map remain unchanged.

Completion means the requirements pass deterministic and failure-path tests with an independently generated reconciliation showing one—and only one—terminal result for every accepted batch. This is an evidence and implementation requirement only; it is not production authorization, and the broader Mosaic scale-response cycle remains open.

Post-marriage checklist — Alex and Devika

There is no broad mandatory “marriage update” filing here since neither of you is changing names or combining health coverage.

1. Do now / time-sensitive

- Taxes: Since you were married on November 12, you’ll be treated as married for federal tax purposes for all of 2025. Before filing, compare Married Filing Jointly versus Married Filing Separately.[1][2]
- Withholding: Run the IRS withholding estimator for both jobs and submit updated W-4s if needed, particularly since you both work.[1]
- Health insurance: If both current plans remain suitable, no enrollment change is required. If either of you wants to switch or add the other, employer-plan special enrollment generally ends 30 days after marriage — December 12, 2025; Marketplace enrollment generally ends January 11, 2026.[3]
- Beneficiaries: Review and confirm beneficiaries on retirement plans, life insurance, HSAs, and payable-on-death accounts. Naming each other as primary beneficiaries and adding contingent beneficiaries is a sensible default, subject to plan rules.[6][7][8]
- Emergency access: Update employer emergency contacts, medical portals, and relevant release/access settings. Also confirm each of you has the desired New York health-care proxy and agent designation; marriage is specifically a reason to review it.[9]

2. Optional but worthwhile housekeeping

- Insurance: Tell home/renters and auto insurers about any household change, ask about bundling discounts, and review life/disability coverage. Marriage is a review point, not a reason to combine policies automatically.[7][8]
- Banking: Keep separate accounts if that remains your preference. Decide whether you want a shared operating account, and verify any joint-account survivorship or payable-on-death designations with the bank.[10]
- HSA: If either of you has an HSA, review its beneficiary separately; HSAs cannot be joint, and a spouse designated as beneficiary generally receives favorable HSA treatment.[11]
- Records: Secure and scan the certificate. Because neither of you changed names, there is no SSA, DMV, passport, or employer-name-change sequence to complete.[1]

3. Certified copies

Shopping list for 3 adults, with modest leftovers

- 1 fresh 4–4½ lb whole chicken, preferably not larger
- 2 lb Yukon Gold or russet potatoes
- 1 lb green beans
- 1 14-oz can/jar whole-berry cranberry sauce
- 1 stick butter
- 1 pint milk or half-and-half
- Salt, pepper, olive oil, and optional garlic/thyme
- Instant-read thermometer, if you don’t have one
- Foil and shallow storage containers, if needed

Wednesday evening: about 45 minutes

- 7:00–7:05 — Check that the chicken is thawed and refrigerated on a tray. If frozen, keep thawing it in the refrigerator; do not thaw it on the counter.
- 7:05–7:15 — Peel and cube the potatoes; start them in salted water.
- 7:15–7:25 — While the potatoes boil, set out the serving dishes and trim the green beans. Store the beans dry in a covered container lined with a paper towel.
- 7:25–7:35 — Drain and mash the potatoes with butter, milk, salt, and pepper.
- 7:35–7:45 — Spread the potatoes in a shallow container, refrigerate promptly, and cover once chilled. Put the cranberry sauce in its serving bowl or a covered container in the refrigerator.

Thursday cooking sequence

- 1:45–2:25 — Set the table, arrange serving dishes, and clear the kitchen. Keep the chicken and prepared sides refrigerated.
- 2:30–3:00 — Take Kibo on his substantial walk.
- 3:00–3:15 — Heat the oven to 350°F. Pat the chicken dry, season it, place it breast-side up in a roasting pan, and wash/sanitize the preparation area. Don’t rinse the chicken.
- 3:15 — Roast the chicken, unstuffed.
- 4:00 — Anya arrives with dessert; the chicken continues roasting.
- 4:30 — Begin checking the chicken with the thermometer. Check the thickest breast and innermost thigh; both need to reach 165°F. Recheck every 10–15 minutes. If the breast is done first, loosely tent it with foil.
- When the chicken reaches 165°F, likely around 4:45–5:10 — Remove it, tent loosely, and rest for 20–25 minutes.
- During the rest:
  - Reheat the mashed potatoes in a covered saucepan with a splash of milk and butter, stirring until the center reaches 165°F.
  - Cook the green beans in a second saucepan or skillet with butter, salt, and pepper, about 8–10 minutes.
  - Put out the cranberry sauce.
- 5:10–5:20 — Carve the chicken and transfer everything to serving dishes.
- 5:30 — Dinner.

If the chicken is not at 165°F by 5:10, keep roasting it and delay the beans rather than relying on resting heat. Keep reheated food at 140°F or warmer, and don’t leave the chicken or sides sitting at room temperature. After dinner, Kibo’s evening walk can stay around 7:30.

For 2025, the important date is December 31—not the month you married. Because you and Devika were legally married on December 31, your federal filing-status choices are:

- Married filing jointly (MFJ)
- Married filing separately (MFS)

You generally cannot file as Single or Head of Household simply because the wedding occurred in November.[1][2]

Your unchanged legal names are fine. Enter each name as it appears in Social Security Administration records and on the W-2; do not assume either spouse adopted a new surname.[2]

Federal comparison

MFJ — usually the first scenario to test

- One return reports both spouses’ income, withholding, deductions, and credits.
- It often produces lower combined tax. For 2025, the standard deduction is $31,500 for MFJ versus $15,750 for each MFS return.[2]
- It generally preserves credits and deductions that MFS restricts, including education credits and the student-loan-interest deduction. The child/dependent-care credit is also generally more available on a joint return.[5]
- Both spouses generally become responsible for the full tax, interest, and penalties on the joint return—even if the issue came from only one spouse.[4]
- Check whether either employer paid qualifying overtime or tips. Certain new 2025 deductions require a joint return.[2]

MFS — worth comparing, but often less favorable

- Each spouse files a separate federal return.
- It may be useful if liability separation is especially important or if a particular income-based calculation works better separately, but the IRS says most couples save money by filing jointly.[1]
- If neither spouse itemizes, each generally uses the $15,750 standard deduction. If one spouse itemizes, the other generally cannot use the standard deduction.[2][5]
- Important restrictions can include losing the education credits and student-loan-interest deduction, and generally losing the child/dependent-care credit. The earned-income credit is also generally unavailable except under limited rules.[5]
- Shared items still need to be allocated consistently. Filing separately does not mean that household income, bank interest, investments, HSA activity, or joint expenses can simply be ignored.

What to compare in tax software

1. Prepare both MFJ and MFS scenarios through the final preview.
2. Compare the combined federal and New York result—not just one spouse’s refund.
3. Confirm all income and withholding:
   - Both W-2s
   - Interest and dividends
   - Brokerage transactions
   - Retirement distributions
   - HSA activity
   - Unemployment or other 1099 income
4. Test whether MFS would eliminate or reduce:
   - Education credits
   - Student-loan-interest deduction
   - Child/dependent-care benefits
   - Retirement-savings credit
   - IRA deductions
   - Any qualifying 2025 overtime or tips deduction
5. If itemizing, compare mortgage interest, charitable gifts, medical expenses, and state and local taxes. The 2025 federal SALT limit is generally $40,000 for MFJ and $20,000 for MFS, subject to the applicable income limitations.[2]
6. Consider non-tax effects, such as student-loan repayment calculations, financial-aid formulas, or other benefits that may use household income.

New York and New York City

New York generally expects married taxpayers to use the same filing status on the state return as on the federal return:

- Federal MFJ → generally a joint New York return
- Federal MFS → generally separate New York returns

New York has exceptions, especially when one spouse was a New York resident and the other was a nonresident or part-year resident. In that situation, separate New York returns may be required, although the couple may sometimes elect a joint New York return treating both spouses as full-year New York residents.[3]

If both of you lived in New York for all of 2025 and South Slope was your permanent home on December 31, you would generally start with Form IT-201. For Brooklyn, the New York return uses Kings County and includes the New York City resident-tax information.[3] The W-2 address supports the household facts, but by itself does not establish the full-year residency analysis.

Household document checklist

Identity and filing setup

- Marriage certificate or certified marriage record
- Both Social Security numbers and dates of birth
- Each spouse’s exact legal name as used by SSA and the W-2
- South Slope address as of December 31, 2025
- Lease or other address documentation
- New York City school-district name and code, if the software requests it

Income and withholding

- Verify each W-2’s wages, federal withholding, New York State withholding, New York City withholding, retirement contributions, and HSA information
- Confirm that neither W-2 was corrected or duplicated in the software

  - Interest and dividends

  - Retirement accounts
  - HSA distributions
  - Unemployment
  - State tax refunds
  - Other payments
- Records for bonuses, overtime, tips, deferred compensation, or other pay not obvious from the W-2s

Deductions and credits

- HSA Forms 1099-SA and 5498-SA, plus contribution records and Form 8889 information, if applicable
- IRA contribution records
- Form 1098-E for student-loan interest
- Form 1098-T and education-expense records, if applicable

That comparison is meaningful as an initial signal, but not as a final result. It assumes the figures are refunds, rather than amounts owed; first verify the labels in the software.

What commonly creates the difference

1. Different tax-rate calculations

A joint return combines both spouses’ income and applies the married-filing-jointly tax structure. Separate returns divide the income between two returns and apply the married-filing-separately structure. If one spouse earns substantially more, combining the income can sometimes use the tax brackets more efficiently; in other cases, the separate calculation can help.

2. Credits and deductions

Filing status affects which credits and deductions are available, their income limits, and how they are calculated. The IRS specifically identifies filing status as affecting tax owed, credits, and the standard deduction.[1]

For 2025, the standard deduction is $31,500 for MFJ and $15,750 for each MFS return.[7] If both of you use the standard deduction, the combined MFS standard deduction is also $31,500, so the standard deduction alone may not explain the difference. The difference may instead come from tax brackets, credits, income limitations, or how deductions are allocated.

If either W-2 includes qualifying overtime or tips, verify those amounts separately. Certain 2025 deductions for qualified overtime and tips require a joint return.[7]

3. Withholding and refund mechanics

A refund is not the same thing as tax savings. It is generally the difference between total tax liability and payments already made through withholding or estimated payments.

Therefore, compare these separately:

- Total federal tax
- Total New York tax
- Total federal withholding
- Total New York State and New York City withholding
- Credits and deductions
- Final refund or amount due

A larger combined refund could reflect lower combined tax, but it could also be affected by how withholding and other payments are assigned between the two separate returns.

4. Allocation of shared items

On a joint return, all household income and deductions generally appear together. On separate returns, shared items must be assigned consistently between the spouses. This matters particularly for:

- Interest from a joint bank account
- Brokerage income or jointly held investments
- HSA activity
- Joint deductions or payments
- Any income document issued in only one spouse’s name

The missing interest statement is therefore more than a missing small line item: it may also determine which spouse reports the income in the MFS scenario.

How much the missing 1099-INT matters

The comparison should be treated as incomplete until the statement is entered.

The missing statement could affect:

- Taxable interest added to federal and New York income
- Tax-exempt interest reported for federal purposes
- Federal backup withholding, if any
- An early-withdrawal penalty deduction, if any
- Which spouse reports the income if you use MFS
- Whether the added income changes a tax bracket, credit, deduction, or income phaseout

The IRS instructions say taxable interest generally must be reported even if it is not yet reflected on a Form 1099-INT, and the amount should be reconciled to the payer’s records.[4][6]

If the interest amount is small and there is no withholding or penalty, it may not change the overall comparison much. But without knowing the amount, ownership, and boxes on the statement, there is no reliable way to say whether the $1,125 difference is stable. The current result is best viewed as a directional screening result, not a filing-ready conclusion.

Entries and documents to verify first

1. Confirm the projection itself

- Verify that the numbers are refunds, not amounts owed.
- Verify that both scenarios include the same income documents and deductions.
- Compare the combined MFS result, not just one spouse’s separate refund.
- Compare total tax before comparing refund amounts.
- Review the final-preview summaries, not only an early estimate.

2. Confirm filing-status facts

- Legal marriage existed on December 31, 2025. Federal filing status is generally based on marital status on the last day of the year.[1]
- Both spouses’ legal names match Social Security records and the tax documents.
- Both Social Security numbers and dates of birth are entered correctly.
- Confirm each spouse’s full-year New York State and New York City residency.
- If both were full-year New York residents, New York generally uses the same filing status as the federal return. Different-residency situations have exceptions and can require separate New York returns even when the federal return is joint.[3]

3. Verify income and withholding

- Corrected Sphere W-2 is the only active Sphere wage record.
- Hospital W-2 is entered once.
- Wages, retirement contributions, HSA information, federal withholding, New York State withholding, and New York City withholding match both W-2s.
- Missing 1099-INT:
  - Payer
  - Recipient name and SSN
  - Taxable interest
  - Tax-exempt interest
  - Early-withdrawal penalty
  - Federal withholding
  - Whether the account is individual or joint
- Any other bank interest or 1099-OID not yet entered.
- 1099-DIV forms.
- Brokerage 1099-B information and cost basis.
- Retirement distributions and 1099-R forms.
- HSA Forms 1099-SA and 5498-SA, plus the Form 8889 information.
- Unemployment, side income, bonuses, deferred compensation, or other 1099 income.
- Any qualifying overtime or tips that might trigger the 2025 deductions.

4. Verify deductions and credits

- IRA contributions and whether either spouse was covered by an employer retirement plan.
- Student-loan interest and whether MFS would affect the deduction.
- Education expenses and Forms 1098-T, if applicable.
- Marketplace health insurance Form 1095-A, if applicable.
- Child or dependent-care information, if applicable.
- Mortgage interest, property taxes, charitable contributions, and medical expenses if itemizing.
- New York 529 contributions.
- New York renter or other household credits, if applicable.
- Whether either spouse has a prior-year credit, carryforward, or payment that the software allocated incorrectly.

5. Consider the non-calculation issue

MFJ generally means both spouses are jointly and individually responsible for the tax, interest, and penalties on the joint return—even if an error arose from one spouse’s income.[8] That is a separate consideration from which preview produces the larger refund.

Also, after a joint return has been filed, the IRS generally does not allow switching to separate returns after the due date merely because the separate calculation later appears better.[8] That is why the status should be settled only after the missing statement and the other entries are verified.

Bottom line: the current figures suggest a difference, but the missing interest statement prevents treating the $1,125 gap as dependable. Before choosing a status, verify the statement, all income and withholding, the refund-versus-tax labels, New York residency/status fields, and the final MFJ/MFS previews. The other spouse reports their allocated share even though the 1099-INT was not issued under their TIN. Is the bank profile and deposit history enough?

Not by themselves.

The bank profile establishes that the bank issued the $364.27 Form 1099-INT using Alex’s TIN and that Alex was the sole tax-reporting recipient. No. Rehearsal-generation time must not stand in for an authority record’s own source timestamp.

The two times answer different questions:

- Authority/source timestamp: when the authoritative record was created, published, verified, or otherwise observed by its source system.
- Rehearsal-generation time: when Lantern retrieved, transported, or rendered the fixture.

Using the latter as the former would make old or timestamp-less authority data appear current and would conflate provenance with transport timing. The rehearsal time may be retained separately as an observation or attempt timestamp, but it must never participate in freshness evaluation or be presented as the authority record’s timestamp.

The rehearsal question set should therefore assert:

- A timestamp-less authority record produces explicit `unknown` / `missing_provenance` and no inferred authority.
- An old authority record is evaluated using its source timestamp and becomes stale or unavailable according to the existing freshness rule.
- A fresh rehearsal around an old or timestamp-less record does not change that result.
- The rendered result, if permitted, preserves the source timestamp; rehearsal-generation time is separately labeled and non-authoritative.
- No fallback to internal metadata, ingestion time, verification time, or rehearsal-generation time is allowed.

This preserves the established Lantern rule: freshness, provenance, and source timestamp are independent requirements.

No. `rehearsal_generated_at` is the rehearsal/processing time, not the authority record’s source-observation time. Using it as `source_timestamp` would create misleading freshness and ordering provenance, even if `authority_record_id` is retained.

For that case:

```text
authority_record_id: <present ID>
source_timestamp: null
rehearsal_generated_at: <rehearsal time>
```

The reference candidate should remain provenance-incomplete and be rejected or rendered as `unknown` under the existing fail-closed contract. Retaining the ID is useful for traceability, but it does not justify inferring the authority timestamp.

5:50–5:58 — Prep
- Cube 1 large eggplant into roughly 1-inch pieces.
- Halve the cherry tomatoes.
- Drain/rinse 1 can chickpeas.
- Mince 2 garlic cloves; chop a handful of parsley.
- Set out about ¾ cup yogurt, ½ lemon, 2–3 oz feta, and spices.

5:58–6:08 — Brown the eggplant
- Heat 2–3 tbsp olive oil in a large skillet over medium-high.
- Add eggplant, ¾ tsp salt, black pepper, and about ½ tsp cumin or paprika.
- Cook 8–10 minutes, stirring occasionally, until softened and browned. Add another splash of oil if the pan gets dry.

6:08–6:20 — Make the skillet
- Add garlic and cook 30 seconds.
- Add tomatoes, chickpeas, ½ tsp paprika or cumin, a pinch of chili flakes if wanted, and ½ cup water.
- Cover and simmer 10–12 minutes, stirring once or twice, until the eggplant is fully tender and the tomatoes have collapsed.

6:10–6:20 — Couscous
- While the skillet simmers, bring 1 cup water to a boil with ½ tsp salt and 1 tsp olive oil.
- Stir in 1 cup dry couscous, cover, remove from heat, and let stand 5 minutes.
- Fluff with a fork and stir in a little parsley, lemon zest or juice, and black pepper.

6:20–6:25 — Lemon yogurt and finish
- Mix ¾ cup yogurt with 1 small grated or minced garlic clove, 1–2 tbsp lemon juice, a pinch of salt, and enough water to make it spoonable.
- Taste the skillet and adjust salt, pepper, lemon juice, or olive oil. Stir in some parsley.

6:25–6:30 — Serve
- Spoon couscous into bowls and top with the eggplant-chickpea mixture.
- Add lemon yogurt, crumbled feta, parsley, and a final drizzle of olive oil.

Based on your current clearance—no move cap or active forearm restriction, while retaining the longer warmup and gradual load increase—I’d treat these as two different projects rather than assuming the V6 is automatically harder.

Comparison

V5 compression line:
- Higher whole-body demand: sustained tension, squeezing, and keeping the hips close.
- The heel-hook transition is the key learning problem. Fatigue will make the heel slide, hips sag, and hands overwork.
- Best trained with short, deliberate movement rehearsals and longer rests.
- Likely the more systemically tiring project.

V6 vertical line:
- Lower pulling demand, but higher precision demand.
- Small edges and deliberate feet reward quiet feet, body positioning, and patience rather than force.
- Finger and foot-placement quality may deteriorate before you feel generally exhausted.
- Treat it as a technical/finger-intensive project, not an “easy” project because it is vertical.

Use four total project sessions, alternating which climb is primary. Leave roughly 48 hours, or at least a symptom-free next morning and good general recovery, between hard project sessions.

General warmup for every session: 15–20 minutes

1. 3–5 minutes of easy general movement: brisk walking, cycling, or similar.
2. 3–5 minutes of comfortable wrist, forearm, shoulder, hip, and ankle mobility.
3. 7–10 minutes of very easy climbing:
   - large holds and open-hand grips first;
   - vertical or slab terrain;
   - downclimb where practical;
   - gradually introduce normal pulling, edging, and one or two easy heel hooks.
4. Finish with two easy rehearsal moves resembling the day’s project, but at roughly half effort.

Do not count the project’s crux attempts as part of the warmup.

Attempt spacing

- Easy movement drills: 60–90 seconds between repetitions.
- Normal project attempts: 3–4 minutes.
- A near-limit attempt or full sequence: 5–7 minutes.
- During the rest, identify one change for the next attempt. Do not make several changes at once.
- If an attempt produces the same failure twice without giving new information, stop repeating the whole problem and isolate the movement.

Session 1: Map both projects

Primary goal: learn the movement, not test your grade.

After the warmup:

- V5: 2–3 controlled attempts, stopping before the heel-hook transition becomes desperate.
- V6: 2–3 controlled attempts, emphasizing quiet feet and pauses rather than reaching the finish.
- Between attempts, identify:
  - V5: where the hips leave the wall, when the heel begins to load, and whether the transition requires turning the knee or moving the torso first.
  - V6: which foot placement makes the next hand move feel stable and whether you are pulling before establishing your feet.

Movement practice:
- V5: rehearse the compression position and heel-hook transition separately on easier holds. Practice setting the heel, bringing the hips in, rotating through the hook, and only then changing the upper body.
- V6: repeat the key foot sequence with “silent feet”—place each foot once, pause briefly, and avoid readjusting unless it genuinely cannot hold.

Stop point:
- End the project portion after 5–6 serious attempts total across both climbs, or sooner if you have identified the main movement and your attempts begin repeating the same tired error.
- Finish with easy climbing and leave without a max-effort attempt.

Session 2: V5 primary, V6 secondary

After the warmup:

V5:
- 2–3 low-intensity rehearsals of the heel-hook transition.
- 3 quality attempts on the crux or the largest linked section.
- One longer link attempt only if the preceding attempts were technically clean.
- Rest 4–6 minutes between serious attempts.

Useful V5 cues:
- “Hips first, hands second.”
- Establish the heel before committing to the transition.
- Keep the heel active without violently pulling with it.
- Exhale through the compression instead of holding your breath and over-gripping.

V6:
- 2–3 technical attempts, preferably stopping before the most fatiguing section.
- Use a different foot-placement experiment on each attempt, not a different strategy everywhere.

Stop point:
- End the V5 block after two consecutive attempts in which the heel-hook transition becomes less precise, even if you still feel capable of trying again.
- End the whole session when your grip begins substituting for body position on V6, or after about 6–8 serious attempts total.
- The session should finish with the sense that you could have made one more good attempt.

Session 3: V6 primary, V5 secondary

After the warmup:

V6:
- 2 easy rehearsals of the crux sequence.
- 3–4 serious attempts with 4–6 minutes of rest.
- Focus on one technical variable per attempt:
  1. exact foot placement;
  2. hip position and balance;
  3. timing of the weight transfer;
  4. linking the sequence without rushing.

Useful V6 cues:
- Place the foot before pulling.
- Keep the center of mass over the feet.
- Pause long enough to feel the position, but do not hang passively on the small edges.
- Use the least aggressive grip that lets you move accurately; do not turn every attempt into a maximum crimp test.

V5:
- 2–3 maintenance attempts or isolated heel-hook rehearsals.
- Keep these below the intensity that would compromise the V6 work.

Stop point:
- Stop the V6 project when foot placements become noisy, you start readjusting repeatedly, or you pull through a position that was previously controlled.
- Do not add attempts merely because the problem is vertical. Small-edge precision is often the first thing lost to fatigue.

Session 4: Link and assess

This is an assessment session, not necessarily a sending session.

After the warmup:

- Choose the project that feels more informative or more likely to produce a clean link and start there.
- Give each project:
  - one rehearsal or partial attempt;
  - two high-quality serious attempts;
  - a third attempt only if the prior two were still technically sound.
- Rest 5–7 minutes before a full-sequence or near-limit attempt.
- If you send one, avoid immediately chasing a harder “bonus” effort. Use the remaining time to repeat the crux at lower intensity or climb easy problems well.

Stopping point:
- Stop a project after two attempts with no meaningful technical improvement.
- Stop the session after one clean send, one clearly improved link, or when both projects require compensatory pulling and rushed feet.
- A successful session can be “I learned the heel-hook timing” or “I found the stable left-foot placement,” even without topping either problem.

A simple rule for all four sessions

Each attempt should answer one question. If you cannot state what changed before the next attempt, rest longer or stop attempting the whole climb. Preserve one good attempt in reserve rather than spending the session proving that fatigue can make the same movement worse.

Continue to use your established step-back criteria: stop if discomfort exceeds 2/10, if symptoms last 30 minutes, or if symptoms appear the next morning; in those cases, reduce the next exposure and contact your clinician as previously directed.

- Do 2–3 low-intensity finishing rehearsals from the last two or three moves.
- Practice the final setup rather than repeatedly pulling hard:
  - establish the feet before reaching;
  - keep the heel active through the transition;
  - bring the hips in and maintain body tension;
  - pause briefly to confirm the finishing foothold;
  - reach without allowing an avoidable foot cut.
- Rest 60–90 seconds between rehearsals.

Hard attempts:

1. Attempt 1: full link with the main cue “finish with the feet, not a last-second pull.” Use the exact final-foot placement you believe is most reliable.
2. Rest 5–7 minutes.
3. Attempt 2: change only one finishing variable—such as earlier hip positioning, keeping the heel engaged longer, or delaying the final reach until the feet are settled.
4. Rest 5–7 minutes.
5. Attempt 3: take it only if the first two attempts were still controlled and your movement quality has not deteriorated. Treat it as the final assessment attempt, not a desperation burn.

V5 stopping points:

- Stop after two attempts with the same final foot cut unless you have a specific, credible adjustment for the third.
- Stop immediately if the heel slips, the hips sag, or you begin pulling through the transition rather than executing it.
- Stop the V5 block after a send or a clearly improved, controlled finish. Do not add a bonus max attempt after either result.

Rest 8–10 minutes between projects. Inspect and clean your fingertips without filing or otherwise trying to conceal tenderness.

V6 vertical line — precision and skin-protection block

Hard-attempt cap: 2 total. No third quality burn this session.

Before attempting:

- Check each fingertip for tenderness, hot spots, thinning skin, or a developing split.
- If the skin is already tender during the rehearsal, skip the hard attempts and do only easy technical climbing or end the session.

Drills:

- Do 2–3 short quiet-foot rehearsals, preferably on easier terrain or by isolating the opening sequence.
- Place each foot once, pause long enough to establish balance, and avoid readjusting.
- Use the least aggressive grip that allows the move; do not turn the drill into a crimp-strength test.
- Rest 60–90 seconds between repetitions.

Hard attempts:

1. Attempt 1: prioritize exact foot placement and keeping your center of mass over the feet. Move slowly enough that the opening sequence remains quiet.
2. Rest 5–7 minutes and reassess your fingertips.
3. Attempt 2: make one technical change only—such as a different foot angle, hip position, or timing of the weight transfer.

V6 stopping points:

- Stop after two attempts regardless of whether you still have general energy.
- Stop sooner if fingertip tenderness increases, the skin feels hot or raw, or you begin gripping harder to compensate.
- Also stop if feet become noisy, repeated readjustments appear, or a previously controlled move becomes rushed.
- Do not use tape or extra chalk to push through skin warning signs.

Finish with 5–10 minutes of easy, comfortable climbing or movement. The session is successful if you achieve a clean V5 finish, make a meaningful finishing adjustment, or execute the V6 sequence with quieter feet and preserved skin—even without a send.

Keep the established forearm boundaries unchanged: stop if discomfort exceeds 2/10, if symptoms persist for 30 minutes, or if symptoms appear the next morning. Any next-morning reaction means the progression was not tolerated and the next climbing exposure should step back rather than advance.

“Tenant breached the 64 pending-batch limit” implies the tenant exceeded the cap, but the control is designed to prevent that. The metric measures retryable refusals before acceptance; it does not establish that pending batches exceeded 64.

Suggested copy:

Panel title: “Tenant backpressure”

Alert text: “Tenant received retryable queue-full responses before acceptance; per-tenant pending capacity was unavailable.”

If the dashboard has a verified tenant-scoped diagnostic, you could add:

“Pending batches remain capped at 64 per tenant; excess work was refused before acceptance.”

This preserves the distinction between the enforced pending limit and pre-acceptance refusal activity.

Attribution problem

The signal comes from the service’s admission control, not from evidence of tenant intent or misuse. Reaching the 64-pending-batch cap triggers retryable backpressure before the work is accepted. Therefore, the signal establishes an operational capacity event only; it does not establish customer fault, excess cost, or failure of accepted work. Pre-acceptance refusals should remain separate from accepted-work accounting.

Kibo’s Halloween setup for tomorrow, 5:30–8:30 PM

Before 5:30 PM

- Use the quietest interior room, away from the apartment door and hall—ideally a bedroom or bathroom he already finds comfortable.
- Put his bed, water, and a familiar toy there. Close the door and use a TV, fan, or white noise to soften the doorbell and hallway noise.[1]
- Add a sturdy baby gate in the hallway as a second barrier if practical, but do not rely on the gate instead of the closed room door.[1]
- Do not tether Kibo to furniture or a doorknob. Use his properly fitted harness and leash only when an adult is actively holding him during a move.
- Store all chocolate, chocolate baked goods, and candy bags in a high, closed cabinet or latched container. Darker chocolate is generally more hazardous.[2]
- Store sugar-free candy, gum, mints, and anything labeled xylitol, birch sugar, or wood sugar in the same secured location. Xylitol can be extremely dangerous even in small amounts.[3]
- Put a lidded trash can behind a closed door or inside a cabinet. Wrappers go directly into it—never into an open bowl or grocery bag. Foil and cellophane wrappers can cause intestinal blockage if swallowed.[1]
- Keep Kibo at 2.25 cups total for the day. Count any training kibble or settling rewards inside that amount; give no candy, table food, or extra Halloween treats.

Answering the door

- Choose roles in advance: one “door person” and one “Kibo person.”
- Before every door opening, the Kibo person confirms that the safe-room door is fully latched and the gate is in place.
- Keep Kibo out of the entryway. The door person answers, hands out candy, then closes and latches the apartment door before doing anything else.[1]
- If Kibo must be moved, do it before opening the apartment door: harness and leash on, with one adult holding the leash. Never open the door while he is loose near the threshold or in the hall.
- Use a sign or silence the doorbell if possible. If the barrier cannot be maintained, stop answering until Kibo is secured.
- After 8:30, inspect the entryway and hallway for dropped candy, wrappers, and decorations before letting him out.

If you suspect ingestion

1. Treat any possible chocolate, sugar-free/xylitol candy or gum, raisin-containing candy, or wrapper ingestion as an immediate call to your veterinarian, emergency veterinary clinic, or poison control—even if Kibo looks normal. Chocolate risk depends on the type and amount, while wrappers add a blockage risk.[1][2][3]
2. Remove Kibo from the area and keep the package, ingredient list, and remaining candy. Note the product, estimated amount, time, type of chocolate or sweetener, and whether a wrapper was swallowed.
3. Call ASPCA Poison Control at (888) 426-4435, available 24/7, or your veterinarian/emergency clinic.[4]
4. Do not induce vomiting or give hydrogen peroxide, salt, oil, laxatives, food, or human medication unless a veterinarian or poison-control professional specifically directs you. For suspected xylitol ingestion, do not give anything orally unless directed.[3]
5. Go straight to an emergency veterinarian for collapse, trouble breathing, seizures, marked weakness, pale/gray/blue gums, repeated vomiting, inability to keep water down, tremors, severe agitation, repeated unproductive retching, a swollen or painful abdomen, or choking. Do not wait for symptoms after suspected xylitol ingestion, since low blood sugar can develop quickly and serious liver injury can follow.[3]
6. If string or ribbon is visible from his mouth or anus, do not pull it. Call a veterinarian immediately.

Sources:

[2] https://vcahospitals.com/know-your-pet/chocolate-poisoning-in-dogs
[3] https://vcahospitals.com/know-your-pet/xylitol-toxicity-in-dogs

Because dinner was refrigerated within 90 minutes, these leftovers were handled well. Assuming the refrigerator is at 40°F/4°C or colder:

Storage plan

- Keep refrigerated: only what you realistically expect to eat Friday through Sunday. Use shallow, covered containers.
- Freeze now: any amount beyond those planned portions—especially extra loaf and mashed potatoes. Freezing today gives better quality than waiting.
- Roasted green beans can be frozen safely, though they’ll become softer; keep a Sunday portion refrigerated and freeze the rest if needed.
- Standard fruit apple pie can stay refrigerated for the weekend or be wrapped and frozen slice-by-slice. If it contains custard, cream, or meringue, keep it refrigerated rather than relying on freezing for quality.

Dates

- Dinner was Thursday, November 26.
- Refrigerated leftovers are generally good for 3–4 days, so Sunday, November 29 is a comfortable target for eating the refrigerated portions.
- Monday, November 30 is the outer four-day limit. Freeze anything still refrigerated by then rather than keeping it longer; freezing now is preferable if you already know it won’t be eaten.
- Frozen leftovers remain safe indefinitely at 0°F/-18°C, though quality is best within roughly 2–6 months.

Reheating the loaf

1. Thaw a frozen portion overnight in the refrigerator when possible.
2. Slice it before reheating.
3. Put slices in a covered baking dish with a tablespoon or two of water, broth, or sauce.
4. Heat at 325°F, covered, until the center reaches 165°F—usually about 15–25 minutes for slices, longer for a thick piece.
5. For a quicker method, microwave covered at 50–70% power in 60–90-second intervals, turning or rearranging between intervals.

Reheating the potatoes

- Microwave: Add a splash of milk, cream, broth, or water and a little butter if desired. Cover, heat in short intervals, and stir well between intervals until steaming hot and at least 165°F.
- Stovetop: Warm covered in a saucepan over low heat, adding liquid gradually and stirring often to prevent scorching.
- Don’t repeatedly reheat the whole container—warm only the serving you’ll eat.

The key safety endpoint for both dishes is 165°F throughout; covering them while reheating helps them retain moisture.

Repair is the clear choice: the backpack is otherwise structurally sound, and a $28 slider replacement restores the main-compartment zipper in three business days. It saves $90—about 76% less than the $118 replacement. Until then, avoid putting the compartment under tension.

Assuming this is a bag or luggage compartment, repair is usually the more practical choice if the bag itself is sound.

Repair is preferable when:
- The slider is loose, cracked, or has come off.
- The pull tab broke.
- The zipper is separating but the teeth and fabric tape are intact.
- A repair shop can replace only the slider rather than the whole zipper.

Choose replacement if:
- Teeth are missing, bent, or repeatedly separating.
- The zipper tape is torn or pulling away from the fabric.
- The box/pin at the zipper end is damaged.
- The surrounding fabric or seam is ripped.
- A slider replacement would only be a short-lived fix.

For the few days before repair, the least damaging temporary method is:

1. Empty or lightly load the compartment.
2. Close the zipper gently; do not force a slider past a snag.
3. If there are two zipper pulls, place them together and connect their pull holes with a small split ring, smooth mini-carabiner, or short piece of soft cord.
4. If there is only one pull, tie that pull loosely to a nearby sewn-in loop or strap using ribbon, shoelace, or another soft cord. The cord should prevent the pull from moving, not pull tightly on the zipper.
5. For better security, put a broad luggage strap or soft webbing strap around the entire bag. This supports the compartment without putting point force on the zipper.

Avoid glue, adhesive tape across the zipper, safety pins through the zipper tape, pliers, or a tightly cinched cable tie. Do not sew or pierce the zipper area as a temporary fix. If the zipper is already separating or teeth are damaged, keep the compartment’s contents in an inner pouch and rely on the external strap rather than trying to make the zipper carry tension.

One-day rain plan for Kibo

12:30 PM — Brief bathroom break
- Use his usual front-clip harness and leash; choose the quietest nearby side streets.
- Keep it to about 5–10 minutes: bathroom first, then a little sniffing if the footing is safe.
- Avoid flooded curb sections, deep puddles, slick leaves, exposed areas under trees, and places with falling branches or poor visibility.
- Towel-dry his coat, legs, belly, and paws when you return; check briefly for grit or irritation.

1:00–3:00 PM — Indoor rest and scent work
- Let him settle with water available.
- Do one easy scent game: hide a few pieces of his regular kibble around one room, use a familiar snuffle mat, or roll kibble loosely in a towel for him to find.
- Keep it calm rather than turning it into vigorous indoor exercise.

3:30 PM — Second brief bathroom break
- Repeat the same quiet side-street route for roughly 5–10 minutes.
- If the gusts intensify, rain becomes driving, or the route is becoming slippery or obstructed, make this a quick out-and-back potty break.

4:00–5:00 PM — Low-key training
- Use regular kibble from his daily allowance for two or three 3–5-minute sessions: name response, hand target, settle on a mat, “find it,” or simple position changes.
- Stop while he is still engaged. Add a chew, lick mat, or quiet rest afterward if those are familiar options.

Food total
- Breakfast: 1 cup, assuming his normal breakfast has already been served.
- Training: reserve up to 0.25 cup of regular kibble, counted as his training treats.
- Dinner: 1 cup.
- Total: 2.25 cups for the day. Do not add extra treats on top.

Around 5:30–6:30 PM — Evening sequence
1. Give Devika a chance to get home and decompress; Kibo’s routine does not need to wait on her exact arrival.
2. Feed Kibo his 1-cup dinner at his usual time and refresh his water.
3. After a short settling period, take a 10–15-minute sniff-and-potty loop if the rain and wind have eased. Use the front-clip harness, stay on quieter side streets, and turn back early for worsening gusts, standing water, slick footing, or any sign Kibo is uncomfortable.
4. Dry him thoroughly and keep the rest of the evening quiet—dinner, calm indoor time, and rest.
5. Do one final quick potty break at his usual bedtime, shortening it to the minimum safe bathroom outing if conditions are still poor.

This is a weather adjustment for one day, not a new exercise baseline. Resume his normal longer outing on the next suitable day, provided his energy, gait, appetite, and bathroom habits remain normal.

Bounded cross-system review for Cardinality Guardrails PR 448

Decision: Request changes. Production remains unchanged.

The candidate has a cross-system semantic failure: an omitted `pending_batches` field is decoded as numeric zero, then exported as:

- `limit_state="below_limit"`
- `source_timestamp=clock.Now()`

That converts unavailable telemetry into a current, measured zero-load observation. The metrics-router operating panel can therefore show a tenant as healthy and fresh even though no queue-state measurement exists.

Failure modes

1. Missing telemetry is reported as healthy
   - Absent `pending_batches` becomes `below_limit`.
   - Operators cannot distinguish zero pending batches from missing queue data.

2. Freshness is falsely renewed
   - `clock.Now()` describes export time, not the age of the underlying observation.
   - Repeated exports can make an indefinitely missing source appear continuously current.

3. Alerts and stale-data detection can be suppressed
   - A panel or alert keyed to `limit_state` may clear or remain green.
   - Any consumer using `source_timestamp` for freshness will accept the fabricated timestamp.

4. Recovery and diagnosis become ambiguous
   - When telemetry resumes, consumers cannot tell whether the prior state was genuinely below the limit or merely unavailable.
   - Incident timelines lose the distinction between “measured zero” and “no measurement.”

Required correction

Preserve field presence through decoding. At minimum:

```text
pending, present := decode(snapshot.pending_batches)

if !present {
    emit(
        limit_state="unknown",
        source_timestamp=<original source timestamp, or explicit unavailable/null>,
    )
    return
}

state := "below_limit"
if pending >= 64 {
    state = "at_limit"
}

emit(
    limit_state=state,
    source_timestamp=<timestamp of the observed queue state>,
)
```

Do not use the export clock as `source_timestamp` for an absent or stale source. If the contract requires a timestamp field, represent unavailable provenance explicitly rather than inventing one. Keep export/emission time separate from source-observation time.

Minimum acceptance evidence

- Omitted `pending_batches` produces `limit_state="unknown"`, never `below_limit`.
- Explicit `pending_batches=0` produces `below_limit`.
- `pending_batches=63` produces `below_limit`.
- `pending_batches=64` produces `at_limit`.
- Missing telemetry does not receive the current export time as `source_timestamp`.
- Repeated exports while the field remains absent do not refresh source freshness.
- A stale source remains distinguishable from a current measured zero.
- The metrics-router panel and any alert logic preserve the unknown state rather than treating it as healthy.
- Tests cover absent, explicit zero, threshold boundary, stale, and resumed telemetry cases.

For your 2027 HDHP, the distinction is:

- Covered preventive visit: The clinician’s routine preventive-exam claim. If coded and processed as eligible in-network preventive care, the plan should cover it at $0 member cost.
- Separately processed lab work: The lab may submit its own claim, sometimes under a different provider, date, or claim number. It may also be covered at $0 if it is an eligible preventive screening, but it is not automatically covered just because it occurred during a preventive visit. Diagnostic tests, follow-up tests, noncovered panels, frequency-limit issues, or out-of-network processing can create cost-sharing.
- EOB: The insurer’s Explanation of Benefits. It explains what was billed, the allowed amount, insurer payment, adjustments, denial/reason, and assigned patient responsibility. It is not a bill and does not itself require payment.
- Actual provider bill: A payment request from the clinician or lab. Pay it only after reconciling it with the final EOB(s).

Verification sequence before paying:

1. Wait for the final EOB for the visit and any separate final EOB for the lab. Record each claim number, service date, provider, procedure code, billed amount, allowed amount, and patient responsibility.
2. Confirm whether each line was processed as preventive, diagnostic, or another service; confirm network status and whether the EOB says the claim is final.
3. Match the provider bill to the EOB: same provider or lab, service date, services, claim, adjustments, and balance. The bill should generally equal the EOB’s patient-responsibility amount—not the billed amount or the allowed amount.
4. If they match and the amount is assigned to you, pay the provider or lab through its official billing channel.
5. If there is no EOB yet, the EOB is pending, or the bill exceeds the EOB responsibility, do not assume the amount is payable. Ask billing to place it on hold while it is reconciled.

Ask about coding or a mismatch when:

- The preventive visit is processed as diagnostic or has unexpected cost-sharing.
- Lab work that should be preventive is processed as diagnostic, noncovered, or subject to the deductible.
- The provider bill is higher than the EOB responsibility, or the EOB assigns $0 but the provider demands payment.
- The bill contains a service, date, provider, or code not shown on the EOB.
- The insurer says the coding, diagnosis, modifier, screening frequency, or network information caused the result.

Ask the provider for an itemized reconciliation and whether the submitted code accurately reflects what was performed; ask the insurer whether the EOB is final and what specifically caused the patient responsibility. Request correction only if the submitted information is factually wrong—do not ask anyone to change accurate coding merely to obtain coverage.

Christmas dinner menu for 3 adults, with one lunch leftover

Main: Spinach-ricotta stuffed shells
- 20 jumbo shells, allowing for a few broken shells
- 15 oz ricotta
- 10 oz frozen chopped spinach, thawed and squeezed very dry
- 1 egg
- 6–8 oz shredded mozzarella
- ½ cup grated Parmesan
- About 3 cups marinara sauce
- Italian seasoning, garlic, salt, and pepper

This should yield roughly 15 shells for dinner and 5 shells for one lunch, with enough sauce and cheese to keep the leftovers good.

Side 1: Lemony garlic green beans
- 1½ lb green beans
- 2 garlic cloves
- 1 lemon
- 1 tablespoon butter or olive oil
- Optional: pinch of red-pepper flakes

Side 2: Citrus greens salad
- 5 oz arugula or mixed greens
- 2 oranges, peeled and segmented
- ⅓ cup walnuts or pecans, optional
- Simple dressing: 3 tablespoons olive oil, 1 tablespoon red-wine vinegar, 1 teaspoon Dijon mustard, salt, and pepper

Anya’s pie can be served afterward. I would skip bread unless you want it; the shells and pie make this plenty substantial.

Consolidated shopping list

Produce
- 1½ lb green beans
- 5 oz arugula or mixed salad greens
- 2 oranges
- 1 lemon
- 1 bulb garlic

Dairy and eggs
- 15 oz ricotta
- 8 oz shredded mozzarella
- 4 oz Parmesan
- 1 egg
- Butter, if preferred for the green beans

Frozen
- 10 oz frozen chopped spinach

Pantry
- 1 package jumbo pasta shells, at least 20 shells
- 1 32-oz jar marinara sauce
- Olive oil
- Red-wine vinegar
- Dijon mustard
- Walnuts or pecans, optional
- Italian seasoning or dried oregano
- Salt, black pepper, and optional red-pepper flakes

Preparation timeline

Christmas Eve, or Christmas morning

- Cook 20 shells in salted water until just shy of al dente. Rinse briefly under cool water so they stop cooking.
- Mix the ricotta, spinach, egg, half the mozzarella, half the Parmesan, ½ teaspoon Italian seasoning, salt, and pepper.
- Spread about 1 cup marinara in a metal 9-by-13-inch baking dish. Fill and arrange the shells, cover with the remaining sauce, and top with the remaining mozzarella and Parmesan.
- Cover tightly and refrigerate.
- Make the salad dressing, wash and dry the greens, trim the beans, and refrigerate everything separately.

Christmas Day

1:00–1:30 PM
- Set out serving dishes and make sure the stuffed-shell dish is covered and refrigerated.
- Segment the oranges and prepare the dressing if not already done.

2:00 PM
- Do the last kitchen setup before Kibo’s outing. Keep the casserole chilled.

2:15–3:30 PM
- Take Kibo on the longer midafternoon outing.
- The exact window can shift, but aim to be back about an hour before dinner.

3:30 PM
- Return and preheat the oven to 375°F.
- Bake the covered, chilled shells for 25 minutes, then uncover and bake another 15–20 minutes, until bubbling and hot through the center.

4:05 PM
- Start the green beans: sauté the garlic briefly, add the beans and a splash of water, cover for 4–5 minutes, then uncover and finish with lemon juice, olive oil or butter, salt, and pepper.

4:15 PM
- Toss the greens, orange segments, and nuts with just enough dressing to coat.

4:20–4:25 PM
- Remove the shells and let them rest for 5–10 minutes.
- Transfer the beans and salad to serving dishes.

4:30 PM
- Serve dinner. Refrigerate the leftover shells and any remaining beans promptly after the meal; the salad is best eaten that evening.

If using a glass baking dish, do not put it straight from the refrigerator into a hot oven. Use a metal pan, or let the dish warm gradually according to its manufacturer’s instructions.
